entries.meaning: Higher than something, with air in between. That single geometric fact generates every other sense: higher on a map, higher on a measuring scale, higher in a hierarchy, and — by a short moral leap — too high in character to stoop to something. The one thing above never means is touching.
examples: A hawk circled above the parking lot. (1)
She keeps the good glasses above the microwave. (1)
Denver is a mile above sea level. (2)
The reservoir is twelve feet above normal. (2)
Temperatures stayed above forty all week. (3)
Anything above two hundred dollars needs a second signature. (3)
A lieutenant is one grade above a sergeant. (4)
She put the team above her own record. (4)
He is not above taking credit for someone else's work. (5)
No one in that office is above suspicion. (5)
The exceptions noted above apply only to renewals. (6)
Everything above this line is a draft. (6)

entries.pronunciation note: uh-BUV; the first syllable is always the reduced /ə/, and there is no further weak form
entries.русский: выше, над — расположен выше без соприкосновения; выше по шкале, рангу или в тексте
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund in the fixed not above doing X idiom (she's not above lying). Never a finite clause — write above the line that says "total", not above it says "total". Also an adverb (the sky above), an adjective (the above figures), and a noun (see the above); the preposition alone takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] above [noun phrase] · [noun] above [noun phrase] · not above [verb-ing] · above all
entries.contrast: The above/over line is height versus alignment. Above asserts only that one thing is higher; over adds vertical alignment and often covering or crossing. A lamp can be above or over the table, but a blanket can only be over it, and a village can be above the valley without being over anything. For measurements and scales, above is the word — above sea level, above average, above freezing — while over takes quantities and counts (over fifty people). Against on: on requires contact, above forbids it.
entries.see also: over, atop, below, on, on top of

entries.meaning: The low end of something, treated as a place you can be at. The phrase does three jobs that the simple prepositions cannot: it picks out a specific part of an object rather than a relation to the whole of it, it works on flat things laid out in reading order (pages, columns, lists, charts) as readily as on vertical ones, and by an old metaphor it names the thing lying underneath a situation as its cause.
examples: He waited at the bottom of the hill with the sled. (1)
There is a drain at the bottom of the window well. (1)
Add the subtotal at the bottom of the third column. (2)
The disclaimer runs at the bottom of every page. (2)
Divers found the truck at the bottom of the quarry. (3)
The good scissors are at the bottom of that drawer somewhere. (3)
Our team spent the whole season at the bottom of the standings. (4)
A billing error was at the bottom of the entire dispute. (5)
I suspect plain boredom is at the bottom of it. (5)

senses.head: Underneath a pile, a container, or a body of water

senses.head: In the last position in a ranking or a standing

senses.head: Being the underlying cause of a situation

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — only bottom keeps a beat: at reduces to /ət/, the to /ðə/, and of to /ə/ before a consonant, so at the bottom of the stairs comes out /ət ðə ˈbɑɾəm ə ðə ˈstɛrz/ · uht-thuh-BAH-duhm-uh-thuh-STAIRZ, with the medial /t/ of bottom flapped to a /d/-like tap
entries.русский: внизу, на дне, у подножия — в самой нижней точке; в конце списка; в основе (причина)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — at the bottom of the page, at the bottom of it. No gerund and no that-clause: ✗ at the bottom of falling behind, ✗ at the bottom of that he lied. To hang a finite clause on it you need a noun to carry the clause: at the bottom of the claim that he lied.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] at the bottom of [noun phrase] · [noun] at the bottom of [noun phrase] · [sign / add / start] at the bottom of [page or column] · be at the bottom of [trouble] (cause)
entries.variants: in the bottom of — a different preposition, and the distinction is worth keeping: at the bottom of the drawer is the low end of it, in the bottom of the drawer is inside it, down at the bottom. The motion form is to the bottom of (sank to the bottom of the lake, get to the bottom of this).
entries.contrast: Against below and under, which are simple prepositions naming a relation between two things; at the bottom of names a part of one thing and puts you at it — below the stairs is underneath them, at the bottom of the stairs is standing on the floor they end at. Against at the foot of, the anatomical twin, which is fixed to a short list of landmarks: at the bottom of the list is right and ✗ at the foot of the list is odd, while both work for stairs and hills. Against beneath, which is literary and cannot name a part at all.
entries.see also: at the top of, at the foot of, below, under, beneath, at

entries.meaning: The lower end of something that the language treats as having a body. The metaphor is old and it is closed: English decided long ago which things have feet, and a learner who extends the phrase to a new noun will usually be wrong. Within its list, though, it is the ordinary word — no American calls the place where a hillside meets flat ground anything but the foot of the hill.
examples: We left the car at the foot of the trail and hiked in. (1)
A stone marker stands at the foot of the bluff. (1)
She was waiting at the foot of the stairs with her coat on. (2)
The dog barked at the foot of the attic ladder for an hour. (2)
He folded the quilt at the foot of the mattress. (3)
There is a cedar chest at the foot of the bed. (3)
The footnotes run at the foot of each page rather than at the end. (4)
Add the totals at the foot of the column. (4)
Someone had propped a wreath at the foot of the statue. (5)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — at /ət/, the /ðə/, of /ə/ before a consonant, with only foot stressed: at the foot of the bed is /ət ðə ˈfʊt ə ðə ˈbɛd/ · uht-thuh-FUUT-uh-thuh-BED. The vowel of foot is the lax /ʊ/ of book, never the /u/ of boot
entries.русский: у подножия, в ногах — у основания горы, лестницы, памятника; в ногах кровати
entries.register: neutral, with a faint literary tilt in the landscape senses
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund and no that-clause: ✗ at the foot of climbing the ridge. And the object is restricted — it has to be a thing the body metaphor already covers (a bed, a hill, a cliff, a staircase, a page, a column, a cross), which is why ✗ at the foot of the argument fails where at the bottom of the argument succeeds.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] at the foot of [noun phrase] · [noun] at the foot of [noun phrase] · at the foot of the bed / the stairs / the hill / the page
entries.variants: the motion form is to the foot of (walked to the foot of the falls); at the base of is the neutral technical paraphrase for cliffs, towers, and trees
entries.contrast: Against at the bottom of, which is the general-purpose phrase and fits anything with a low end. Foot is the anatomical member of the pair and is frozen to a short list of landmarks — beds, stairs, hills, mountains, cliffs, pages, columns, crosses. Both are right for stairs; only bottom is right for a list or a drawer. Against at the head of, its opposite end. Against below, which relates two things instead of naming a part of one.
entries.see also: at the head of, at the bottom of, below, beneath, under, at

entries.meaning: The upper, leading, or source end of something the language gives a body to. From the physical end it reaches two places the plain vertical words cannot follow it to — the place a river or a valley starts, and the position of the person in charge. What holds the senses together is precedence: whatever is at the head comes first, whether in space, in order, or in rank.
examples: A guide was waiting at the head of the stairs. (1)
Put the extra pillows at the head of the bed. (1)
There is a trailhead at the head of the canyon. (2)
The old mill stood at the head of the creek. (2)
Put the date at the head of the memo, not the foot. (3)
He finished the morning at the head of the leaderboard. (3)
Two motorcycles rode at the head of the funeral procession. (4)
She spent nine years at the head of the school board. (5)
The senator at the head of the delegation refused to comment. (5)

body: Her name was at the head of the waiting list.

senses.head: Leading a procession, a column, or a march
body: The pipers marched at the head of the parade.

senses.head: In charge of an organization, a family, or a delegation
body: She has been at the head of the agency since March.
examples: A guide was waiting at the head of the stairs. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — at /ət/, the /ðə/, of /ə/, with only head stressed: at the head of the table is /ət ðə ˈhɛd ə ðə ˈteɪbəl/ · uht-thuh-HED-uh-thuh-TAY-bul
entries.русский: во главе, в изголовье — у верхнего конца стола или кровати; первым в списке, в колонне
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund and no that-clause: ✗ at the head of running the office — write at the head of the office. As with its opposite, the object is restricted to nouns the body metaphor covers: tables, beds, stairs, lines, columns, valleys, bays, rivers, processions, and organizations.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / sit / stand / march] at the head of [noun phrase] · [noun] at the head of [noun phrase] · at the head of the table / the line / the stairs / the department
entries.variants: the motion form is to the head of (moved to the head of the line); at the top of is the neutral paraphrase for stairs and lists, and in charge of for the authority sense
entries.contrast: Against at the top of, which head can usually replace and which cannot always replace head. Two things belong to head alone. The first is the source of running water: the head of a river, a valley, a bay, or a hollow is where it begins, and the top of the river means nothing. The second is authority: at the head of the department means running it, while at the top of the department means only occupying its highest rung. Against before and in front of: at the head of the line is a position in the line, in front of the line is outside it.
entries.see also: at the foot of, at the top of, above, before, in front of, ahead of

entries.meaning: The high end of something, treated as a place. Like its opposite, the phrase names a part of an object rather than a relation between two objects, and it runs freely over things that are not vertical at all: a page has a top, so does a list, a chart, a batting order, and an hour. What it never does is claim contact — that job belongs to on top of and atop.
examples: She was standing at the top of the stairs with the phone in her hand. (1)
A ranger station sits at the top of the pass. (1)
The date goes at the top of the second page. (2)
Milk was at the top of the shopping list. (2)
Two women at the top of the firm signed the letter. (3)
She finished the year at the top of her class. (3)
The kids were singing at the top of their lungs the whole ride. (4)
He called her name at the top of his voice and got no answer. (4)

body: Put your name at the top of the form.

senses.head: In the leading position of a ranking or an organization
body: The album sat at the top of the chart for a month.

senses.head: In the two volume idioms, at the top of one's lungs and at the top of one's voice

A ranger station sits at the top of the pass. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: also /ət ðə ˈtɔp əv/ in dialects that keep the cot/caught distinction; weak form — at /ət/, the /ðə/, of /ə/ before a consonant, with only top stressed: at the top of the page is /ət ðə ˈtɑp ə ðə ˈpeɪdʒ/ · uht-thuh-TAHP-uh-thuh-PAYJ
entries.русский: наверху, на вершине — в высшей точке; в начале списка; на первом месте в рейтинге
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — at the top of the hill, at the top of it. No gerund and no that-clause: ✗ at the top of finishing the roof, ✗ at the top of that it was late.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] at the top of [noun phrase] · [noun] at the top of [noun phrase] · at the top of [page / list / hour / stairs] · at the top of one's lungs / voice
entries.variants: on top of (see on top of) is a different preposition, not a variant — see the contrast below. The motion form is to the top of; in the top of puts the thing inside (in the top of the closet).
entries.contrast: The pair to keep apart is at the top of and on top of. At the top of the hill is a location — you stand at its high point. On top of the hill is contact with the surface, and it is what a house or a water tower does. You climb to the top of a ladder but you sit on top of a wall. Against above, which is height without any part named, and atop, which is contact on a high surface in a formal register. Against at the head of, which adds the ideas of source and authority that top does not carry. And note that the clock sense — at the top of the hour — is time, not place, and belongs to time.
entries.see also: at the bottom of, at the head of, atop, above, on top of, over

entries.meaning: Resting on the highest surface of something, in contact with it. It is a written word — headlines, captions, nature writing, and real-estate copy love it — and it survives mainly because it is shorter than on top of and grander than on. It also has a small figurative life in the language of rankings and standings.
examples: A single crow sat atop the utility pole. (1)
The chapel atop the hill is visible from the highway. (1)
Snow lay six inches deep atop the woodpile. (1)
She placed the last shingle atop the stack. (1)
The company ended the quarter atop the industry. (2)
He has stayed atop the rankings for three seasons. (2)

senses.head: On the highest surface of a physical thing
body: A weathervane atop the barn.

senses.head: At the top of a ranking or standing (journalistic)
body: The Dodgers finished atop the division.

entries.pronunciation note: uh-TAWP in dialects that keep the cot/caught distinction; the first syllable is already the reduced /ə/ and never takes stress, so there is no further weak form
entries.русский: на вершине, поверх — книжн., газетное; в разговорной речи почти не встречается
entries.register: formal or literary; common in journalism, rare in speech
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only. No gerund, no clause. Atop of is nonstandard — the of belongs to on top of, not to atop.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] atop [noun phrase] · [noun] atop [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] atop [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Atop is on top of compressed into one word, and it is the more formal of the two — no American says atop out loud at the kitchen table. Unlike above, it requires contact; unlike plain on, it insists the surface is a high or prominent one. On the table is neutral; atop the table sounds like a museum label.
entries.see also: on top of, above, over, upon, on

entries.meaning: Lower than something, with no claim about contact or alignment. Like its opposite above, it works on maps and on scales as readily as in the air: downstream is below, downhill is below, and any number smaller than the reference point is below it. It is the everyday word for lower position when nothing is doing any covering.
examples: There is a crawlspace below the kitchen floor. (1)
The clouds sat below the summit all morning. (1)
The town lies just below the reservoir. (2)
Fishing is better below the bridge than above it. (2)
It stayed below freezing for nine days straight. (3)
Her cholesterol is finally below two hundred. (3)
No one below director level saw the memo. (4)
He was two years below me in school. (4)
See the table below for the current rates. (5)
Everything below the dotted line is optional. (5)

entries.pronunciation note: buh-LOH
entries.русский: ниже, под — ниже без соприкосновения; меньше указанного уровня; ниже по тексту
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause. Also an adverb (the deck below, see below) and, in nautical use, an adverb meaning belowdecks; the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] below [noun phrase] · [noun] below [noun phrase] · below [number or level]
entries.contrast: The below/under line mirrors above/over. Below claims only lower position; under adds vertical alignment and often covering or containment. You sleep under a blanket, never below one, and you camp below the tree line, not under it. Measurements and scales take below — below freezing, below zero, below average — while under takes quantities and ages (under thirty, under twenty dollars). Against beneath, which is the same idea in a literary register.
entries.see also: under, beneath, underneath, above, down

entries.meaning: Directly under something, usually with the weight or nearness of the upper thing felt. It is under in a raised register, plus two senses of its own: the surface that conceals something, and the standard that something falls short of. Reach for it when you want the sentence to sound written rather than spoken.
examples: The ice groaned beneath their boots. (1)
Roots had buckled the sidewalk beneath the maple. (1)
Beneath the fresh paint, the wood was rotten. (2)
Beneath all the legal language, the offer is simple. (2)
That kind of gossip is beneath contempt. (3)
He seemed to think manual labor was beneath him. (3)

senses.head: Directly under, often with weight or pressure
body: The porch steps creaked beneath him.

senses.head: Under the surface of, hidden by an appearance
body: Beneath the cheerful tone was real panic.

senses.head: Unworthy of, too low for someone's dignity
body: The remark was beneath her.

entries.pronunciation note: buh-NEETH; the th is voiceless /θ/, not the /ð/ of breathe
entries.русский: под, из-под — книжн. синоним under; также «ниже достоинства» (beneath her)
entries.register: formal or literary
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No finite clause. A gerund appears only in the frozen disdain idiom (beneath answering, beneath discussing) and is rare. Also an adverb (the valley beneath).
entries.pattern: [be-verb] beneath [noun phrase] · [verb] beneath [noun phrase] · beneath [abstract noun] (beneath contempt)
entries.variants: 'neath /niθ/ — a poetic clipping that belongs to verse, hymn, and song lyric ('neath the willow); never write it in prose
entries.contrast: Beneath is the literary member of the under / underneath / below family and is almost never the natural spoken choice: Americans say the dog is under the table, and beneath the table sounds like a novel. What beneath owns outright is the moral sense — beneath contempt, beneath him, beneath her dignity — where under and below cannot go. It also handles the metaphor of a hidden interior better than either (beneath the surface).
entries.see also: under, underneath, below, above, behind

entries.meaning: Positioned higher than something and, characteristically, lined up with it — which is why over slides so easily into the idea of covering. From physical coverage it reaches authority (one person positioned over another), quantity (a number higher than another), preference (one option placed above another), the channel a message travels along, and the far side of any barrier you would have to go over to reach. The positional senses are collected here; the moving, temporal, and topical senses live elsewhere in this catalog.

He pulled the blanket over his head. (2)
There was a tarp over the boat all winter. (2)
A rash had spread over both arms by Tuesday. (3)
Papers were scattered over every surface in the room. (3)
The repair came to a little over nine hundred dollars. (4)
Over half the class failed the first quiz. (4)
No one over her signed off on the change. (5)
He was given authority over both warehouses. (5)
I'd take a long drive over a short flight any day. (6)
The committee chose the local firm over two national ones. (6)
They worked out the terms over the phone in ten minutes. (7)
The alert went out over the emergency channel at four. (7)
She is finally over the worst of the flu. (8)
He is not over the layoff and may not be for a while. (8)
Her cousins live over the border in Nogales. (9)
The next town over the ridge has one gas station. (9)

senses.head: By way of a channel or a medium

senses.head: Past and no longer troubled by

The alert went out over the emergency channel at four. (7)
She is finally over the worst of the flu. (8)
He is not over the layoff and may not be for a while. (8)
Her cousins live over the border in Nogales. (9)
The next town over the ridge has one gas station. (9)

entries.pronunciation note: OH-ver; the second syllable is the r-colored /ɚ/ in all American speech and keeps it even unstressed, so over has no weak form of the kind of and to have — what happens in fast speech is that the whole word loses its beat, not that its vowels change. The r-less /ˈoʊvə/ is British, not an American reduction.
entries.русский: над, поверх, через — прямо над, накрывая или пересекая; больше чем; по (телефону)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund (an argument over paying the bill, no control over spending) and a wh-clause (an argument over who pays, a fight over what to charge) in the dispute and authority senses. Never a that-clause — ✗ an argument over that he should pay; to hang a finite clause on it you need a noun to carry it (an argument over the claim that he should pay). Also an adverb (come over), an adjective (it's over), and a verb particle (think it over, hand it over), none of which takes an object; the preposition always has one.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] over [noun phrase] · [noun] over [noun phrase] · over [number] · [choose/prefer] [X] over [Y] · stranded: the beam it hangs over
entries.contrast: Against above: over implies vertical alignment and permits covering, above asserts only greater height. A tarp goes over the woodpile, never above it. Against on: on is contact and support, over is coverage from the top — the cloth on the table lies flat, the cloth over the table drapes down the sides. Against under, its exact opposite in every sense here. On sense 9, against beyond: over the ridge names a barrier you would cross to get there, beyond the ridge names only what lies farther out and crosses nothing. Note also that over is the most widely distributed word in this catalog: the path sense (jumped over the fence) is in movement and direction, the span-of-time sense (over the summer) is in time, the about sense (a fight over money) is in topic and reference, the bare quantity sense (over fifty) reappears in agent, instrument, and manner, and the preference sense in comparison and opposition. Senses 4 and 6 below are the positional face of those last two and are kept here because they fall straight out of the vertical geometry.
entries.see also: above, under, atop, across, beyond, over (motion), over (time), over (topic)

entries.meaning: Covering something from above, with the covering insisted on. The phrase is a regional doubling — over already means this, and top is added for emphasis the way off of adds of to off. Learners should recognize it, because they will hear it constantly in a wide band of the country, and should not write it, because outside that band it reads as an error rather than as a dialect.
examples: Put a lid over top of the pot or it will spatter. (1)
They poured a new slab over top of the old one. (1)
Somebody laid plywood over top of the opening. (1)
The paint cans are over top of the paint tray. (2)
She wore a wool vest over top of her flannel shirt. (3)
In edited prose: he wore a jacket over top of his sweater → write over his sweater, or on top of his sweater. (3)

senses.head: Covering, spread across the top of
body: She pulled a blanket over top of the couch.

senses.head: Resting on the upper surface of
body: The extra chairs are stacked over top of the freezer.

senses.head: Worn as an outer layer
body: He wears a windbreaker over top of his uniform.

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — of reduces to /ə/ before a consonant, giving OH-ver-TAHP-uh, and in fast speech the whole phrase carries one main beat, on top. Written and said as one word it is overtop of /ˌoʊvɚˈtɑp əv/ · oh-ver-TAHP-uv
entries.русский: поверх, сверху на — разг., региональное (Зап. Пенсильвания, Огайо, Средний Запад)
entries.register: regional and informal American — strongest in Western Pennsylvania, the Ohio Valley, the inland Midland, the Upper Midwest, and Canada. It is ordinary in speech across that belt and it is not an error there, but edited American prose does not use it: copy editors change it to over or on top of.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause: ✗ over top of painting the wall.
entries.pattern: [put / wear / lay / pour / build] [object] over top of [noun phrase] · [be-verb] over top of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: overtop of (one word plus of), overtop (bare, no of — chiefly Canadian: she wore a vest overtop her sweater), and over the top of, which is the fully standard expansion and the safe choice in writing
entries.contrast: It is over with the covering made emphatic, and it adds no meaning the shorter word lacks: a tarp over the woodpile and a tarp over top of the woodpile describe the same tarp, and the second one tells a linguist where the speaker grew up. Against on top of, which requires contact and support from below; over top of covers, with or without touching — you can pour gravy over top of mashed potatoes and hang a sheet over top of a doorway. Against atop, its opposite in register: atop is formal and written, over top of is spoken and regional.
entries.see also: over, atop, above, on top of, on

entries.meaning: Directly lower than something and usually covered by it. That covering is what lets under become the workhorse abstraction of the group: things covered by an authority, by a rule, by a process, or by a heading are all under it. Of the four low-position words, this is by a wide margin the most useful and the most polysemous.
examples: Your keys are under the newspaper. (1)
We waited out the storm under an overpass. (1)
She wore thermals under her jeans. (2)
Put a towel under the pot before you set it down. (2)
Anyone under eighteen needs a signed waiver. (3)
We finished the job under budget for once. (3)
The clinic operates under state supervision. (4)
He served under three different chiefs. (4)
The proposal is still under review. (5)
Two of the three claims are under investigation. (5)
You'll find it filed under "permits." (6)
She published under a pen name for a decade. (6)

senses.head: Directly below and typically covered by
body: The cat is under the bed.

senses.head: Worn or placed beneath another layer
body: He had a T-shirt under his sweater.

senses.head: Less than a number, an age, or an amount
body: Everything on this rack is under twenty dollars.

senses.head: Subject to the authority, rule, or command of
body: The park is under federal jurisdiction.

senses.head: Undergoing a stated process or condition
body: The bridge has been under construction for two years.

senses.head: Classified within a heading or a name
body: The reservation is under Alvarez.
examples: Your keys are under the newspaper. (1)

She wore thermals under her jeans. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: UN-der; the first vowel never reduces, so there is no weak form. What casual American speech does instead is drop the /d/ after the nasal, giving /ˈʌnɚ/ — UN-ner (under the bed → unner the bed). The r-less /ˈʌndə/ is British, not an American reduction.
entries.русский: под — прямо под и обычно накрытый; меньше (числа, возраста); под властью, в процессе
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No finite clause, no gerund — write under the impression that he had paid (the that-clause belongs to impression, not to under), never under he had paid. Also an adverb (the boat went under) and a prefix (underpaid); the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] under [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] under [noun phrase] · under [number or age] · under [authority] · under [process noun] (under review)
entries.contrast: Against below: under aligns and often covers, below only ranks lower. You are under a bridge when you pass through its shadow and below it when you are downstream. Against underneath: underneath is the emphatic, physical form and has none of under's abstract senses — you cannot say underneath new management or underneath thirty. Against beneath: the same relation in a literary register. And note that scales take below (below freezing) while counts and ages take under (under thirty). Under has two other homes: the path sense (rolled under the fence) is in movement and direction, and the bare quantity sense (under fifty) reappears in agent, instrument, and manner.
entries.see also: underneath, beneath, below, over, above, under (motion)

entries.meaning: Beneath the shade that something large casts — and, far more often, beneath the presence, the reputation, or the menace of it. The literal sense is now the rarer one. What keeps the phrase alive is the metaphor: to live under the shadow of a mountain, a mill, a famous parent, or a diagnosis is to have that thing standing over everything you do.
examples: The flock grazed under the shadow of the ridge until noon. (1)
Three benches sit under the shadow of the old oak. (1)
Whole neighborhoods grew up under the shadow of the refinery. (2)
The chapel stands under the shadow of the cathedral wall. (2)
Every quarterback the school produced played under the shadow of that one season. (3)
The negotiations went on under the shadow of a possible strike. (4)
She finished the treatment but still lives under the shadow of the diagnosis. (4)
In modern prose: rewrite under the shadow of the bridge as in the shadow of the bridge unless the elevated tone is wanted. (2)

senses.head: In the shade cast by something
body: They ate lunch under the shadow of the water tower.

senses.head: Immediately beside something large and dominating
body: The village sits under the shadow of the volcano.

senses.head: Overshadowed by a greater reputation, event, or memory
body: He wrote for thirty years under the shadow of his father.

senses.head: Under the continuing threat of something
body: The town lived under the shadow of the mill closing.

senses.head: Under the protection of something powerful (the biblical sense)
body: Under the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge.
examples: The flock grazed under the shadow of the ridge until noon. (1)
Three benches sit under the shadow of the old oak. (1)
Whole neighborhoods grew up under the shadow of the refinery. (2)

In modern prose: rewrite under the shadow of the bridge as in the shadow of the bridge unless the elevated tone is wanted. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — the is /ðə/ and of reduces to /ə/ before a consonant, so under the shadow of the wall is /ˈʌndɚ ðə ˈʃædoʊ ə ðə ˈwɔl/ · UN-der-thuh-SHAD-oh-uh-thuh-WAWL. Two beats only, on un- and shad-
entries.русский: в тени, под сенью — книжн., библ.: рядом с подавляющим; под угрозой; под защитой
entries.register: literary, elevated, and biblical. The 1611 King James Version fixed it in the American ear — under the shadow of the Almighty, under the shadow of thy wings — and it has stayed in that register ever since. In ordinary modern American English the live form is in the shadow of.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund and no clause: ✗ under the shadow of losing the farm — write under the shadow of a foreclosure, or use in danger of losing the farm.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / live / grow up / work] under the shadow of [noun phrase] · [noun] under the shadow of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: in the shadow of — the ordinary modern American form, and the one to write; beneath the shadow of and the metrical clipping 'neath the shadow of (see 'neath) belong to hymns and to nineteenth-century verse
entries.contrast: Against plain under, which is bare geometry; the shadow adds a caster — something large enough to throw one — and with it the whole figurative freight of the phrase. Against beneath, which is literary but has no metaphor of a looming presence built in. Against overlooking, which puts the big thing above and gives it a view; under the shadow of stands beneath it and gives it a threat. And note the register split with in the shadow of: the two are interchangeable in meaning, but an American who writes under in a news story or a memo will sound as if he is quoting scripture.
entries.see also: under, beneath, below, overlooking, underneath, 'neath

entries.meaning: Directly under and covered by, with the covering emphasized. When someone says look underneath rather than look under, they mean the thing is hidden. The only figurative extension it allows is the one that keeps the covering metaphor intact: an outward appearance with something concealed behind it.
examples: There is a whole box of photographs underneath the stairs. (1)
She found the receipt underneath a stack of mail. (1)
Something was rusting underneath the truck. (1)
Underneath the gruffness he is a soft touch. (2)
Underneath the confident delivery, the argument was thin. (2)

senses.head: Directly under and concealed or covered by
body: The spare key is underneath the mat.

senses.head: Behind an outward appearance
body: Underneath all that swagger he is anxious.
examples: There is a whole box of photographs underneath the stairs. (1)
She found the receipt underneath a stack of mail. (1)
Something was rusting underneath the truck. (1)
Underneath the gruffness he is a soft touch. (2)
Underneath the confident delivery, the argument was thin. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: un-der-NEETH; also stressed on the first syllable, /ˈʌndərˌniθ/ UN-der-neeth, when it precedes a noun; the th is voiceless /θ/. No vowel-reducing weak form — the stressed /i/ has nothing to reduce to — but casual speech drops the /d/ after the nasal exactly as it does in under, giving /ˌʌnɚˈniθ/ · un-ner-NEETH
entries.русский: под, снизу под — прямо под и скрытый чем-то; за внешней видимостью
entries.register: neutral, slightly emphatic
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (look underneath) and a noun (the underneath of the car); the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] underneath [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] underneath [noun phrase] · stranded: the mat it was underneath
entries.contrast: Underneath is the emphatic, strictly physical form of under: it insists that the upper thing covers and usually hides the lower one. That is the whole difference, and it is why underneath refuses every abstract sense under has — underneath new management, underneath thirty, and underneath investigation are all wrong. Against beneath, which says the same thing in a literary register, and below, which requires no covering at all.
entries.see also: under, beneath, below, inside, atop

entries.meaning: A formal equivalent of on, identical in meaning and higher in register. It earns its keep in three places: legal and ceremonial prose, a set of fixed phrases that will not take on, and the "immediately after" construction with a gerund, where it is genuinely more idiomatic than on.
examples: A heavy silence settled upon the room. (1)
He laid the wreath upon the marker. (1)
Upon signing, you receive the keys. (2)
Upon further review, the call was reversed. (2)
Wave upon wave of new applications came in. (3)
Once upon a time there was a mill here. (3)

senses.head: On a surface, in formal or literary style
body: A wreath upon the door.

senses.head: Immediately after (with a noun or gerund)
body: Upon arrival, please check in at the desk.

senses.head: In fixed phrases and repeated-noun intensifiers
body: Mile upon mile of empty road.
examples: A heavy silence settled upon the room. (1)
He laid the wreath upon the marker. (1)
Upon signing, you receive the keys. (2)
Upon further review, the call was reversed. (2)
Wave upon wave of new applications came in. (3)
Once upon a time there was a mill here. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: uh-PAWN; weak /əˈpən/ · uh-puhn, and in fast speech the whole word flattens toward /əˈpɑn/ with no stress of its own
entries.русский: на — книжн. и юр. форма on; также «сразу по» (upon arrival) и усиление mile upon mile
entries.register: formal, literary, or legal; also fixed idioms at every register
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund in the "immediately after" sense (upon arriving, upon signing the lease). Never a finite clause — write upon learning that he had left, never upon he had left.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] upon [noun phrase] · [verb] upon [noun phrase] · upon [verb-ing] · [noun] upon [same noun] (row upon row)
entries.contrast: Anywhere upon appears, on is also grammatical. Upon adds no meaning at all — only formality — so choose it for register, for rhythm, or because a fixed phrase demands it (once upon a time, row upon row, upon further review). Overusing it is the clearest sign of writing that is trying to sound official. Against atop, which insists the surface is high; upon makes no such claim. The motion sense (came upon a clearing) is handled in movement and direction.
entries.see also: on, atop, over, above, upon (motion)

entries.meaning: Level with something and beside it. The word is built on breast in its old sense of chest or front, so the picture is two fronts in line: two ships, two horses, two cars, two runners. From there English took the obvious step to information — to be abreast of the news is to be keeping pace with it rather than trailing behind — and that figurative use has almost swallowed the literal one in ordinary American writing.
examples: A second squad car pulled abreast of the truck. (1)
Two riders came abreast of the leader on the last turn. (1)
The ferry passed abreast of the breakwater and turned north. (2)
Once you are abreast of the second buoy, cut the engine. (2)
Doctors are expected to stay abreast of the research. (3)
He reads two trade papers to keep abreast of what his competitors are doing. (3)
Adverb, no object, and therefore not this preposition: the horses came down the stretch three abreast. (1)

senses.head: Side by side with and level with
body: The patrol boat came abreast of the barge.

senses.head: Having drawn level with a point along a route
body: We were abreast of the lighthouse by six.

senses.head: Keeping pace with information; up to date with
body: She keeps abreast of every filing in the case.
examples: A second squad car pulled abreast of the truck. (1)
Two riders came abreast of the leader on the last turn. (1)
The ferry passed abreast of the breakwater and turned north. (2)
Once you are abreast of the second buoy, cut the engine. (2)
Doctors are expected to stay abreast of the research. (3)
He reads two trade papers to keep abreast of what his competitors are doing. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — the first syllable is already the reduced /ə/ and never takes stress, and of drops to /ə/ before a consonant, so abreast of the news is /əˈbrɛst ə ðə ˈnuz/ · uh-BREST-uh-thuh-NOOZ
entries.русский: вровень с, на уровне — бок о бок и наравне; keep abreast of — быть в курсе
entries.register: neutral. The spatial sense is nautical, military, and traffic-technical; the figurative "up to date" sense is neutral to formal and is by far the commoner of the two in American English.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; also a fused relative — a wh-clause standing in for a noun phrase — in the figurative sense: stay abreast of what the committee decides, keep abreast of what is filed. No that-clause (✗ abreast of that the rules changed), and the gerund is marginal: write keep abreast of changes in the rules, not ✗ keep abreast of changing the rules, which says something else entirely.
entries.pattern: [draw / come / pull / run] abreast of [vessel or vehicle] · [be-verb] abreast of [noun phrase] · [keep / stay / remain] abreast of [developments]
entries.variants: abreast with is dated and now rare; bare abreast is an adverb (three abreast, riding abreast) and takes no object at all — that is the form you see on a bike-lane sign
entries.contrast: Against alongside, which asks for parallel orientation but not for the two things to be level; abreast of insists they are side by side and even, front edges lined up, so a car that has drawn abreast of another is exactly beside it and not a length back. Against beside and next to, plain adjacency with no claim about alignment. The figurative sense belongs with the words of information and is developed in topic and reference; it is kept here because it is the same picture — you and the moving thing are level.
entries.see also: alongside, beside, across from, alongside (motion), next to

entries.meaning: On the other side of a street, a room, a table, or any narrow gap, and facing back this way. It is the plainest of the American facing words and the one that has quietly taken over the spatial work of opposite: an address, a seating arrangement, a restaurant's location, and a witness's position are all given with across from. The gap has to be narrow enough to look over — you are across from a neighbor, not across from a state.
examples: They rented the house across from the elementary school. (1)
There is a food truck parked across from the courthouse most days. (1)
We ended up across from an old classmate at the rehearsal dinner. (2)
Sit across from the window so I can see you on the call. (2)
The chart runs across from the summary on page nine. (3)
The lot across from where the cannery stood is a park now. (1)
She lives directly across from the fire station and has stopped hearing the sirens. (1)

senses.head: On the other side of a street or open space from
body: The pharmacy is across from the post office.

senses.head: Seated or standing facing someone over a table or an aisle
body: He sat across from me for the entire deposition.

senses.head: On the facing side of a printed or laid-out spread
body: The photograph across from the title page.
examples: They rented the house across from the elementary school. (1)

She lives directly across from the fire station and has stopped hearing the sirens. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: also /əˈkrɑs frəm/ · uh-KRAHS-frum in cot/caught-merged speech; weak form — from is almost never stressed and reduces to /frəm/ and, in fast speech, to a syllabic /fṛm/, so across from the school runs uh-KRAWS-frm-thuh-SKOOL. The first syllable of across is already /ə/ and reduces no further
entries.русский: напротив, через дорогу от — обычный американский способ сказать «напротив»
entries.register: neutral — this is the ordinary American English way to say "opposite," and it belongs equally to speech and to edited prose
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; also a fused relative introduced by where: across from where the depot used to be, across from where they hold the market. No gerund and no that-clause: ✗ across from parking the car, ✗ across from that the school was there.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] across from [noun phrase] · [noun] across from [noun phrase] · [sit / live / park / stand] across from [noun phrase] · directly / right / just / diagonally across from
entries.contrast: Across from is what Americans say where the British say opposite. The bank across from the courthouse is ordinary American; the bank opposite the courthouse is correct but reads as British or as formal description. Against facing, which adds orientation: two houses can be across from each other while one of them shows the other a blank wall, but a house facing the park is turned toward it. Against bare across, which spans or covers a surface — a bridge across the river is not across from anything. Against kitty-corner from, which is diagonal rather than straight across. And note that the object attaches to from, not to across: it is across from the school, never ✗ across the school from.
entries.see also: opposite, facing, across, kitty-corner from, in front of, next to

entries.meaning: Immediately next to, sharing a border or an edge. The word came into English out of Latin as a surveyor's and geometer's term and it has never lost that flavor: it is what you write when the exact boundary matters, which is why it dominates the language of land, buildings, and diagrams. A recent extension has given it a second life in journalism, where adjacent to an industry or a movement means bordering on it without belonging to it.
examples: The county rezoned the parcel adjacent to the wetlands. (1)
Guests in the room adjacent to the elevator complained about the noise. (1)
Their property is adjacent to federal land on two sides. (1)
Each node is linked only to the nodes adjacent to it. (2)
Store the reagents in the cabinet adjacent to the fume hood. (2)
He described the startup as adjacent to health care rather than part of it. (3)
In speech, the same sentence is ordinary as the garage is next to the alley. (1)

senses.head: Next to and sharing a boundary with
body: The garage is adjacent to the alley.

senses.head: Immediately connected in a system, a sequence, or a diagram
body: The two cells adjacent to the header are locked.

senses.head: Bordering on something without belonging to it (a recent journalistic use)
body: She works in a field adjacent to publishing.
examples: The county rezoned the parcel adjacent to the wetlands. (1)
Guests in the room adjacent to the elevator complained about the noise. (1)
Their property is adjacent to federal land on two sides. (1)
Each node is linked only to the nodes adjacent to it. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — to is /tə/ before a consonant and /tu/ before a vowel, and it is never stressed; the final /t/ of adjacent and the /t/ of to commonly merge into a single held /t/, giving uh-JAY-suhn-tuh
entries.русский: примыкающий к, смежный с — офиц.-техн.: граничащий вплотную, с общей границей
entries.register: formal, technical, and bureaucratic — zoning ordinances and planning documents, real-estate and insurance filings, engineering drawings, medical charts, and academic prose. In speech Americans say next to, and an editor will usually make the same substitution in ordinary writing.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — adjacent to the parcel, adjacent to it. No gerund and no clause: ✗ adjacent to renovating the wing — write adjacent to the wing being renovated. (Adjacent to parking is fine, but only because parking is a noun there, not a gerund governed by to.)
entries.pattern: [be-verb] adjacent to [noun phrase] · [noun] adjacent to [noun phrase] · immediately / directly adjacent to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: bare adjacent is an adjective and takes no object (the adjacent lot, adjacent rooms); adjoining is the near-synonym that insists on a shared wall or boundary; the dependent-adjective use is catalogued in dependent adjectives
entries.contrast: The line between adjacent to and near is contact. Things adjacent to each other touch or share a boundary; things near each other merely are not far apart. A vacant lot adjacent to the school shares a fence line with it; a diner near the school is two blocks away. Against next to, which means the same thing in one register down, and against contiguous with, which is stricter still and demands an unbroken shared border. Against beside, which is about position rather than about property lines, and is the wrong word for a survey.
entries.see also: next to, beside, near, alongside, next door to, close to

entries.meaning: Touching something and pressing on it. Everything in this entry is the resting state that force leaves behind: a thing leaning, a thing braced, a thing outlined by whatever sits behind it. From physical pressure the word generalizes to opposition of every kind, which is why the same syllable covers a ladder on a wall and a vote in a legislature.
examples: Two shovels leaned against the garage door. (1)
He stood with his back against the counter. (1)
The pressed flowers show up beautifully against the dark paper. (2)
Her red coat was the only color against all that snow. (2)
Parking here is against the building rules. (3)
Three of the five directors voted against the merger. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: uh-GAYNST (minority American, standard British); unstressed it reduces to /əˈɡɛn(t)s/ · uh-GENS, with the /t/ squeezed out between the /n/ and the /s/, and in fast speech the first syllable can vanish entirely, giving 'genst
entries.русский: к, об, о — прижавшись вплотную; на фоне (чего-то); против, вопреки; от (страховка)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (a rule against parking here, advised against going). Never a finite clause — write against the claim that he lied, not against he lied.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / lean / prop / rest] against [noun phrase] · [noun] against [noun phrase] (backdrop) · against [verb-ing] · stranded: the wall it was leaning against
entries.contrast: Against is the contact-under-pressure preposition, and that pressure is what separates it from its neighbors. On is contact with support from below; against is contact with force from the side. Next to and beside are adjacency with no contact at all: the ladder beside the wall is standing free, the ladder against the wall is leaning on it. For the backdrop sense, nothing else will do — dark against the sky cannot become dark on the sky. The forcible-motion sense (threw it against the door) is in movement and direction, and sense 3, opposition proper, is developed at length in comparison and opposition.
entries.see also: beside, next to, on, alongside, against (motion)

entries.meaning: Beside and parallel to, close enough to be lined up with. Its nautical origin still governs the physical sense — you pull alongside a dock the way a hull comes to rest against a pier. The figurative senses keep the parallelism intact: people who work alongside each other are doing the same kind of thing at the same time, as equals rather than as one under the other, and once the equality drops away what is left is bare simultaneity — a document released alongside another one.
examples: The tugboat eased alongside the freighter. (1)
There is a drainage ditch alongside the whole east fence. (1)
A photographer jogged alongside the lead runner. (1)
He learned the trade alongside his father. (2)
The new system will run alongside the old one until June. (2)
She finished the degree alongside working two jobs. (3)
The findings were published alongside a lengthy rebuttal. (3)
The tax cut passed alongside a two-year spending freeze. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: uh-lahng-SYD in cot/caught-merged speech; stress shifts to the first syllable before a noun in fast speech
entries.русский: рядом с, вдоль — параллельно бок о бок; наравне с кем-то; одновременно с
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund in the "at the same time as" sense (studied alongside working nights). No finite clause of any kind, and never a that-clause. Also an adverb (a tug pulled alongside), which takes no object at all; the preposition always has one.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / pull / run] alongside [noun phrase] · [verb] alongside [noun phrase] · alongside [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Alongside adds parallel orientation to the plain adjacency of beside and next to: it wants two long things lying the same way, which is why it started life on the water and still sounds right with boats, trains, roads, and rows. A chair beside the desk is fine; a chair alongside the desk implies the chair is lined up with it. Alongside of is redundant — drop the of. And it is always one word.
entries.see also: beside, along, next to, near, with

entries.meaning: Near; close to. The word says nothing that near does not, and it existed for the reason most poetic forms exist — it gave a writer an extra unstressed syllable and an archaic color. Its interest to a modern reader is historical: it shows the a- prefix still alive and productive at a date when it had already frozen inside aboard and atop.
examples: Nineteenth-century verse: she would not walk anear the water after dark. (1)
Dialect fiction: there's a good spring anear the old orchard. (1)
The flock grazed anear the barrow all that summer. (1)
Ballad diction: he laid him down anear the churchyard wall. (1)
Modern rendering: anear the river becomes near the river — the archaic form has no place in current prose. (1)
Adverb, and therefore not this preposition: the storm came anear and passed over. (2)

senses.head: Adverb, with no object: near at hand

entries.pronunciation note: two syllables, stress on the second; the first is already the reduced /ə/ and never takes stress, so there is no further weak form. The vowel of the stressed syllable is the /ɪ/ + /r/ of near, not the /i/ of knee
entries.русский: близ, подле — устар., поэт.
entries.register: archaic and poetic. It belongs to Romantic and Victorian verse and to the dialect writing of the same century — Tennyson, Swinburne, Hardy, and the ballad collectors. An American meets it in a poetry anthology or a hymnal, never in prose written after about 1900. Do not present it as a modern option.
entries.type: compound (the worn-down Old English an "on, in" + near)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause. It is also an adverb (a rider drew anear), which takes no object — and the adverb is the commoner of the two even in the period that used the word.
entries.pattern: [verb of position or motion] anear [noun phrase] · [noun] anear [noun phrase] · anear (adverb, no object)
entries.contrast: Against near, the live word and the only one to write today. Anear belongs to a whole family of a- forms in which the prefix is that old an "on, in": aboard, atop, astride, abaft, athwart, anigh, anear. Some of that family survived into ordinary English and some did not; anear and anigh are on the losing side, and the difference between them is only that anear is built on near and anigh on nigh.
entries.see also: anigh, near, nearby, hard by, atop, afore

entries.meaning: Near; close to. It is the same archaic a- + adjective pattern as anear, built on nigh instead of on near, and it had the same job: a spare syllable and an old-fashioned sound. It is listed here so that a reader who meets it in a ballad or a hymn can identify it as a preposition and give it an object, rather than mistaking it for an adverb.
examples: Ballad diction: no living soul came anigh the tower. (1)
Nineteenth-century verse: the herd would not graze anigh the fence. (1)
Dialect fiction: don't you go anigh that dog. (1)
Hymn diction: keep me anigh the shepherd's path. (1)
Modern rendering: anigh the mill becomes near the mill — there is no current use of the older form. (1)
Adverb, and therefore not this preposition: the hour drew anigh. (2)

senses.head: Near, close to (archaic and poetic)
body: He would not come anigh the fire.

senses.head: Adverb, with no object: near at hand
body: Winter draws anigh.

entries.pronunciation note: two syllables, stress on the second; the -gh is silent, exactly as in nigh and high; the first syllable is the reduced /ə/ and there is no further weak form
entries.русский: близ, подле — устар., поэт.; ещё реже, чем anear
entries.register: archaic and poetic, and rarer than anear — chiefly nineteenth-century verse, ballad imitation, and dialect writing. It is dead in modern prose and reads as costume.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause. Also an adverb (he came anigh), which takes no object.
entries.pattern: [verb of position or motion] anigh [noun phrase] · anigh (adverb, no object)
entries.contrast: The base word nigh has outlived its own compound: nigh survives in well-nigh, nigh on, and nigh unto, while anigh did not survive at all. Against anear, which is the same formation on near and is slightly the commoner of the two in verse. Against near, the modern word, and hard by, the other archaic proximity phrase an American is likely to meet in period writing.
entries.see also: anear, near, hard by, nearby, afore, 'neath

entries.meaning: At the side of something, close by. It is the plainest adjacency word in English and carries no implication of contact, alignment, or facing. Two idioms have drifted away from the literal sense and are worth learning whole: beside the point, meaning irrelevant, and beside oneself, meaning overcome by an emotion.
examples: There is a bench beside the trailhead. (1)
Park beside the blue truck and walk up. (1)
The first draft looks amateurish beside the final version. (2)
A two-hour delay is nothing beside what they went through. (2)
Whether he meant it is beside the point. (3)
She was beside herself when the dog came back. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: buh-SYD
entries.русский: рядом с, возле — сбоку от; по сравнению с; не путать с besides «кроме того»
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — beside me, never beside I. No clause, no gerund. Unlike besides, it is never an adverb and never a conjunct: you cannot write Beside, it's late.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / sit / stand / walk] beside [noun phrase] · [noun] beside [noun phrase] · beside the point · beside [reflexive] (beside himself)
entries.contrast: Beside and besides are different words, and confusing them is the single most common error in this entire category. Beside is position — at the side of. Besides is addition or exception — in addition to, apart from. The test is substitution: if next to fits, the word is beside (sit beside me); if in addition to or apart from fits, the word is besides (Besides me, only two people came). Beside also differs from alongside, which demands parallel alignment, and from against, which demands contact.
entries.see also: besides, next to, alongside, near, by

entries.meaning: Turned toward something and looking at it across an intervening space. The word has quietly taken over the work American English has been withdrawing from opposite, and it does that work with the orientation made explicit, which is why floor plans, seating charts, and listings reach for it so often. It stays close to its verb: whatever does the facing is understood to have a front.
examples: They asked for a room facing the courtyard. (1)

Two lots facing the water sold in the first week. (1)
All the offices facing the parking lot get afternoon glare. (2)
The bleachers facing the visitors' bench were empty by the fifth. (2)
The map on the page facing the index is out of date. (3)
The photograph facing the title page was taken in 1911. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: FAY-sing; two syllables, stress on the first, and no weak form — like every participial preposition it keeps the shape of the verb it came from
entries.русский: лицом к, выходящий на — обращённый в сторону чего-либо (окна, фасад, места)
entries.register: neutral; the standard word in real-estate, architectural, seating, and travel description
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — facing the park, facing us. No clause, no gerund. One warning is worth the whole entry: the company is facing a recall is the verb face in the progressive, not this preposition. The test is substitution — if opposite or across from can replace it without touching the rest of the clause, it is the preposition (a cabin facing the lake → a cabin across from the lake); if only confronting fits, it is the verb.
entries.pattern: [noun] facing [noun phrase] (the seats facing the stage) · [be-verb] facing [noun phrase] · [sit / stand / park] facing [noun phrase] · [page / plate] facing [page number]
entries.contrast: Facing is the participial member of the opposite / across from group, and it is the one that states orientation outright. Opposite and across from only put two things on either side of a gap; facing says which way the thing is turned. A house can be across from the park and still show it a blank wall, but a house facing the park looks at it. Against before, the formal and largely ceremonial word for the same geometry. Against the near-twin overlooking, which adds height and a downward view — a room overlooking the harbor is above it, a room facing the harbor need not be. And against toward, which is orientation with motion implied; facing is orientation at rest. (Note the spelling there: toward is the American form and towards the British one, and the same split runs through amid/amidst, among/amongst, and around/round in this file.)
entries.see also: overlooking, opposite, across from, across, before, toward, in front of

entries.meaning: Directly opposite; right beside; up against. The dialects that kept it use it for any close confrontation of two things, and context decides which of the three readings is meant. It is included here as a reading aid rather than as a usage recommendation: the modern American writer has across from, beside, and against, and should use them.
examples: Dialect fiction: the church sits forenenst the schoolhouse. (1)
Oral history: they built the new cabin forenenst the spring. (1)
Appalachian speech: come sit forenenst me where I can hear you. (2)
Scots usage: the two farms lie forenenst one another across the burn. (1)
Ulster usage: he had his back forenenst the door the whole time. (3)
Modern rendering: forenenst the barn becomes across from the barn, beside the barn, or against the barn, depending on which of the three is meant. (1)

body: The smokehouse stood forenenst the barn.

senses.head: Right beside, alongside
body: He set his chair forenenst the stove.

entries.pronunciation note: also /fərˈnɪnst/ · fuhr-NINST (spelled forninst) and /fɔrˈnɛnt/ · for-NENT (spelled fornent). Stress falls on the second syllable in every variant and the first reduces to /fɚ/, which is the weak form you will hear in running dialect speech: fuhr-NENST
entries.русский: напротив; вплотную к — диал. (шотл., ольстерское, аппалачское) и устар.
entries.register: regional and archaic. It is Scots and Ulster Scots, northern English, and — in this country — the Scots-Irish inheritance of Appalachia, western Pennsylvania, and the rural Midland. An American meets it in dialect fiction, in folk-song and oral-history transcription, and in the speech of older rural speakers; it does not appear in edited American prose, and a reader outside that belt will not know it.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause. It is also used adverbially in some dialect writing, with no object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / sit / stand / build] forenenst [noun phrase] · [noun] forenenst [noun phrase]
entries.variants: fornent, forninst, fornenst, forenent — all the same word, and the spelling in any given text tells you which dialect the writer was transcribing. The related anent survived on its own into legal and jocular English, but it drifted to mean "concerning," not "opposite."
entries.contrast: The word is worth an entry because it covers three relations that modern English splits between three different prepositions — facing (opposite, across from), alongside (beside), and in contact with (against) — and a reader who assumes only the first will misread half its occurrences. Against anent, its own descendant, which kept the form and changed the meaning. Against hard by, the other proximity word an American meets mainly in period text: hard by is literary and English, forenenst is spoken and Scots-Irish.
entries.see also: across from, opposite, beside, against, hard by, facing

entries.meaning: Immediately beside; very close to. The phrase is a fossil of a much older adverbial hard, and it survives only because writers occasionally want its weight. Where near leaves the distance vague, hard by closes it entirely: a cottage hard by the church is at the churchyard wall, not down the lane.
examples: Period narrative: their cottage was hard by the churchyard wall. (1)
A historical marker: the first mill was built hard by this crossing in 1774. (1)
Guidebook prose: the abbey ruins lie hard by the river path. (1)
Older fiction: he took lodgings hard by the university gates. (1)
Scriptural cadence: they camped hard by the well and waited. (1)
Modern rendering: hard by the station becomes right next to the station or just beside the station. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: two full vowels, with the main stress on by; neither word reduces, and that is part of what makes the phrase sound deliberate — by is the one preposition here that keeps its full /aɪ/ even in a compound
entries.русский: совсем рядом с, подле — устар., книжн.
entries.register: archaic and literary. Shakespeare and the King James Version put it in the language, nineteenth-century narrative kept it, and it now survives as a conscious literary flourish and in British topographical description. An American meets it in older fiction, in guidebook prose reaching for period color, and in historical-marker English.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause. Bare hard by also occurs adverbially in older writing (a mill stood hard by), with no object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / stand / lie / live] hard by [noun phrase] · [noun] hard by [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The hard here means "closely," not "with difficulty." It is the same adverb as in hard on his heels, hard aground, hard aport, and hard upon, and reading it as difficult is the standard misparse. Against near and close to, the everyday words: hard by is closer than either — it means immediately beside, with nothing in between. Against beside, which says the same thing in a modern register, and nigh unto, the other archaic proximity phrase.
entries.see also: near, beside, nearby, anear, close to, next to

entries.meaning: Near; in the space surrounding something. The phrase exists because officialdom needs a way to be approximate on purpose, and both of its senses do that job — the spatial one refuses to fix a distance, and the numerical one refuses to fix an amount. Outside that setting it is padding, and the test is simple: if near fits, use near.
examples: Residents in the vicinity of the plant were asked to stay indoors. (1)
Two aircraft were operating in the vicinity of the field at the time. (1)
Fishing is prohibited in the immediate vicinity of the dam. (1)
Witnesses placed him in the vicinity of the intersection around nine. (1)
The settlement is expected to be in the vicinity of two million. (2)
Attendance was in the vicinity of four hundred. (2)
In ordinary prose: a diner in the vicinity of the courthouse is better written a diner near the courthouse. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — everything but sin is unstressed: in /ɪn/, the /ðə/, the first syllable of vicinity /və/, and of /ə/ before a consonant. The medial /t/ is flapped, so the ordinary American pronunciation is in-thuh-vuh-SIN-uh-dee-uh
entries.русский: поблизости от, в районе — офиц.: язык сводок и отчётов; также «примерно» о сумме
entries.register: formal and official. It is the standard phrase in police blotters and incident reports, aviation and marine advisories, environmental impact statements, insurance claims, and real-estate filings — the places where an American actually meets it. In ordinary prose it is five words doing the work of near, and American editors cut it.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun in the spatial sense; a quantity in the approximation sense (in the vicinity of forty thousand dollars). No gerund, no clause: ✗ in the vicinity of closing the road.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / occur / be seen] in the vicinity of [place] · in the vicinity of [amount] · in the immediate vicinity of [place]
entries.variants: in the neighborhood of is the colloquial twin and is used mainly for the quantity sense (in the neighborhood of two hundred dollars); in the area of and in proximity to are the other bureaucratic equivalents
entries.contrast: Against near, which says the same thing in one syllable and is almost always the better choice. What the longer phrase buys is a deliberate vagueness that official writing sometimes wants: a report that places a suspect in the vicinity of the building has committed to less than one that places him at it. Against around and about for the quantity sense, which are shorter and unmarked. Against in the area of, which is the same padding with a different noun.
entries.see also: near, around, nearby, close to, beside, adjacent to

entries.meaning: Diagonally opposite; across an intersection rather than straight across a street. It is one of the few genuinely American place prepositions, and its geometry is precise enough to be useful: given a four-way intersection, one corner is across from you, one is kitty-corner from you, and the fourth is simply next door. The spelling and the first syllable will tell a linguist which half of the country the speaker comes from.
examples: There is a taqueria kitty-corner from the high school. (1)
We waited kitty-corner from the courthouse until the parade passed. (1)
Southern usage: the feed store sits catty-corner from the depot. (1)
She grew up kitty-corner from the fire station and never got used to it. (1)
The old desk sat kitty-corner from the window to catch the light. (2)
Formal writing: the annex is diagonally across from the main building, not kitty-corner from it. (1)
Adverb, no object, and therefore not this preposition: the rug is laid kitty-corner. (2)
