entries.pronunciation note: the catty- form is /ˈkæti/ · KAT-ee; weak form — from is never stressed and reduces to /frəm/ or to a syllabic /fṛm/, so the whole phrase runs to one main beat on KIT: KIT-ee-korn-er-frm
entries.русский: наискосок от — разг., амер.: по диагонали через перекрёсток
entries.register: informal and regional American, and fully standard within American speech; unknown in British English, where a reader will simply not recognize it. It belongs to speech, letters, and dialogue rather than to formal writing, where diagonally across from is the safe form.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / sit / live / park] kitty-corner from [noun phrase] · [noun] kitty-corner from [noun phrase] · kitty-corner to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: catty-corner from, catercorner from, cater-cornered from, kitty-cornered from, catty-cornered from — and every one of them also takes to in place of from. The regional split is real: kitty-corner is Northern and Western, catty-corner Southern and Midland. The original is catercorner, from the dialect adverb cater "diagonally," which is French quatre — the four spots on a die — and neither cats nor kittens ever had anything to do with it. Bare kitty-corner is an adverb (the store sits kitty-corner) and takes no object.
entries.contrast: Against across from, which is straight across: the deli across from the bank faces it over one street, while the deli kitty-corner from the bank is across the intersection and one street over, on the diagonal. Against opposite, which cannot express the diagonal at all. Against diagonally across from, the plain-English equivalent — longer, unregional, and the right choice when the reader may not be American.
entries.see also: across from, opposite, facing, next to, at the corner of, near

entries.meaning: Not far from, in space, in time, or on a scale of condition. It is the vaguest of the proximity words and that vagueness is the point: near the airport commits to nothing about how near. Its gradability is what sets it apart from every other preposition in this file, and it is the reason near survives in a class that otherwise refuses comparison.
examples: There's a decent diner near the courthouse. (1)
Sit nearer the front if you want to hear. (1)
The fire started somewhere near the fuse box. (1)
It was near midnight before anyone left. (2)
Near the end of the season he tore a hamstring. (2)
She was near tears by the time she finished. (3)
The bid came nowhere near what we needed. (3)

senses.head: Not far from in space
body: They live near the reservoir.

senses.head: Not far from in time
body: Near the end of the movie she walks out.

senses.head: Close to a state, a condition, or a number
body: The company came near bankruptcy twice.
examples: There's a decent diner near the courthouse. (1)
Sit nearer the front if you want to hear. (1)
The fire started somewhere near the fuse box. (1)
It was near midnight before anyone left. (2)
Near the end of the season he tore a hamstring. (2)
She was near tears by the time she finished. (3)
The bid came nowhere near what we needed. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: NEER; one syllable; the vowel is the /ɪ/ + /r/ sequence, not the /i/ of knee. No weak form — near keeps its full vowel even unstressed.
entries.русский: около, близ — недалеко в пространстве или во времени; близко к состоянию или числу
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; also a fused relative — a wh-clause standing in for a noun phrase — in the degree use: nowhere near what we needed, not anywhere near what it cost. ✗ Never a that-clause, and a gerund is marginal at best: came near winning is idiomatic, but ✗ near finishing the report is not. ✗ Alone among the simple prepositions, near is gradable and inflects for degree — nearer the door, nearest the exit — a leftover from its life as an adjective. It is also an adjective (a near miss), an adverb (don't come near), and a verb (the project neared completion).
entries.pattern: [be-verb] near [noun phrase] · [noun] near [noun phrase] · nearer / nearest [noun phrase] · near to [noun phrase] · nowhere near [noun phrase]
entries.variants: near to (chiefly British and slightly formal in American English; bare near is the American default)
entries.contrast: Near and close to are interchangeable in most sentences; near is shorter and takes the comparative directly (nearer the fire, where you would need closer to the fire). Against by, which means immediately beside — stand by the door puts you at it, stand near the door leaves you a few feet away. Against beside, which is adjacency with no distance at all. And note that nearby is not a preposition in careful American English — nearby the station should be near the station.
entries.see also: nearby, close to, next to, beside, by

entries.meaning: Close at hand. It is listed here because learners reach for it as a preposition and American editors take it back out. Treat it as an adjective and an adverb, and hand the prepositional work to near. Its inclusion in a preposition dictionary is a warning label, not an endorsement.
examples: We ate at a taqueria nearby. (1)
Is there a gas station nearby? (1)
A nearby fire station handled the call. (2)
Two nearby counties reported the same outage. (2)
Nonstandard: they camped nearby the lake. Standard: they camped near the lake. (3)
Nonstandard: the office is nearby the courthouse. Standard: the office is near the courthouse. (3)

senses.head: Adverb: at a short distance, with no object
body: There's a hardware store nearby.

senses.head: Adjective before a noun: located close at hand
body: They evacuated three nearby buildings.

senses.head: Preposition (nonstandard in American English): near
body: Nearby the river — write near the river instead.
examples: We ate at a taqueria nearby. (1)
Is there a gas station nearby? (1)
A nearby fire station handled the call. (2)
Two nearby counties reported the same outage. (2)
Nonstandard: they camped nearby the lake. Standard: they camped near the lake. (3)
Nonstandard: the office is nearby the courthouse. Standard: the office is near the courthouse. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: neer-BY; stressed on the second syllable as an adverb (a diner is nearby), on the first as an attributive adjective, /ˈnɪrˌbaɪ/ NEER-by (a nearby diner)
entries.русский: поблизости, близлежащий — как предлог в амер. англ. нестандартно, пишите near
entries.register: neutral as adjective and adverb; the prepositional use is nonstandard in American English
entries.complement: As a preposition it takes a noun phrase — but do not use it that way. Nearby the station is attested and is regularly flagged as an error by American editors; write near the station. In its standard lives it takes no object at all: adjective before a noun (a nearby town), adverb after the verb (they live nearby).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] is nearby (adverb) · a nearby [noun] (adjective)
entries.contrast: The rule is short: near takes an object, nearby does not. A store near the school and a nearby store are both correct; a store nearby the school is the error. This is the cleanest illustration in the file of the test that runs through the whole class — a preposition has an object, an adverb stands alone. Compare near, which is a true preposition; the two-word close by behaves exactly like nearby and takes no object either.
entries.see also: near, next, close to, beside, next to, around

entries.meaning: Immediately beside, with nothing in between. The word is the superlative of the old nigh — nigh, near, next — and it once did prepositional work freely. American English has handed that work to next to and kept bare next for its adjective and adverb duties. The one exception is the clothing phrase next the skin, which survives in older writing and in outdoor and tailoring usage, and even there next to the skin is now more common.
examples: British or nineteenth-century: she took the chair next the window. American: the chair next to the window. (1)
British or nineteenth-century: the church stands next the courthouse. American: next to the courthouse. (1)
Outdoor usage: silk worn next the skin dries fastest. (2)
Tailoring usage: the lining sits next the skin and takes the wear. (2)
Adjective, not this preposition, and no to is possible: we leave next Tuesday. (3)
Adverb, not this preposition, and no object at all: read the second paragraph next. (3)

senses.head: Immediately beside (archaic in American English; current in British English)
body: He sat next the fire all evening.

senses.head: In the fixed phrase next the skin: in direct contact with the body
body: Wear a wool layer next the skin.

senses.head: Word-class note: with no object it is not this preposition at all
body: Who is next?
examples: British or nineteenth-century: she took the chair next the window. American: the chair next to the window. (1)
British or nineteenth-century: the church stands next the courthouse. American: next to the courthouse. (1)
Outdoor usage: silk worn next the skin dries fastest. (2)
Tailoring usage: the lining sits next the skin and takes the wear. (2)
Adjective, not this preposition, and no to is possible: we leave next Tuesday. (3)
Adverb, not this preposition, and no object at all: read the second paragraph next. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: one syllable. No weak form — the vowel is already the short /ɛ/ — but the final cluster routinely loses its /t/ before another consonant, so next the wall comes out /nɛks ðə ˈwɔl/ · NEKS-thuh-WAWL. The same /t/-loss is what gives next to its ordinary spoken shape, NEKS-tuh
entries.русский: рядом с, подле — как предлог устар. в амер. англ.; современная норма — next to
entries.register: archaic in American English. The bare preposition is still current in British English and was ordinary in American writing through the nineteenth century; today it survives here in one fixed phrase and nowhere else. Write next to.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause. In its three ordinary modern lives next takes no object at all — adjective (next week, the next street), adverb (what happens next), noun (the next of them) — and that is the test: the preposition is the only one of the four with something after it that it governs.
entries.pattern: [sit / stand / lie] next [noun phrase] (archaic, and to be avoided) · next the skin (the one surviving fixed phrase)
entries.variants: next to is the American form and the only one to write; next door to narrows it to buildings; nearest covers the superlative (the seat nearest the door)
entries.contrast: This entry is a warning label of exactly the kind nearby carries, and the rule is the mirror image of that one. There, the word takes no object and learners give it one; here, the word can take an object and American English has stopped letting it. He sat next the fire is British or Victorian; Americans write next to the fire. Watch the word-class trap too: next Tuesday and the next exit are the adjective, which never takes to, so ✗ next to Tuesday means something quite different — beside a person named Tuesday. Against beside, alongside, and by, all of which are live American prepositions for the same position.
entries.see also: next to, beside, nearby, near, alongside, by

entries.meaning: Facing something from the other side of a space between. The space matters: things opposite each other are separated and turned toward one another, which is why the word works for seats at a table, buildings on a street, and actors sharing a scene. Americans keep the second of those senses and quietly hand the first to across from.
examples: She took the chair opposite mine. (1)
The hotel stands opposite the train station. (1)
There is a small park opposite the school gates. (1)
She was cast opposite an actor she had never met. (2)
Playing opposite him was the best part of the job. (2)

senses.head: Facing, on the other side of a space (chiefly British in this use)
body: The pharmacy is opposite the library.

senses.head: As the counterpart of another performer
body: He starred opposite Meryl Streep.
examples: She took the chair opposite mine. (1)
The hotel stands opposite the train station. (1)
There is a small park opposite the school gates. (1)
She was cast opposite an actor she had never met. (2)
Playing opposite him was the best part of the job. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: AH-puh-sit; the final syllable is reduced in every American pronunciation
entries.русский: напротив — звучит по-британски, в амер. англ. обычнее across from; также «в паре с» об актёре
entries.register: neutral, but the spatial preposition sounds British or formal in American English
entries.type: simple (functioning as preposition, adjective, adverb, and noun)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adjective (the opposite side), a noun (the opposite of true), and an adverb (they sat opposite).
entries.pattern: [be-verb] opposite [noun phrase] · [noun] opposite [noun phrase] · [act / play / star] opposite [person] · opposite to / from [noun phrase]
entries.variants: opposite to, opposite from (both acceptable; bare opposite is the standard prepositional form)
entries.contrast: For the spatial sense, American English says across from, or facing when the orientation matters. The bank across from the courthouse is the ordinary American sentence; the bank opposite the courthouse is correct but reads as British or as formal description. What is fully American is the casting sense — she played opposite Denzel Washington — which no other preposition covers. Against across, which only requires spanning or being on the other side; opposite adds facing.
entries.see also: across from, across, facing, overlooking, over against, before, near, in front of

entries.meaning: Directly opposite, facing across a space — and, by a natural extension that has outlived the original, set beside something for the sake of the contrast. The spatial sense is a museum piece. The contrastive one is alive but narrow: it belongs to writing that is defining a term by holding it up next to its opposite.
examples: King James cadence: he sat over against the treasury and watched. (1)
Older narrative: the two houses stood over against each other across the lane. (1)
Modern rendering: over against the church becomes across from the church. (1)
Theology: the creature is understood only over against the creator. (2)
Criticism: she reads the late poems over against the early ones. (2)
Social theory: the individual is constituted over against the group. (2)
Plainer alternative: over against the earlier estimate is usually better as compared with the earlier estimate. (2)

senses.head: Directly opposite; facing across a space (archaic and biblical)
body: They pitched their tents over against the city.

senses.head: In contrast with; set beside for comparison (formal and scholarly)
body: He defines freedom over against necessity.
examples: King James cadence: he sat over against the treasury and watched. (1)
Older narrative: the two houses stood over against each other across the lane. (1)
Modern rendering: over against the church becomes across from the church. (1)
Theology: the creature is understood only over against the creator. (2)
Criticism: she reads the late poems over against the early ones. (2)
Social theory: the individual is constituted over against the group. (2)
Plainer alternative: over against the earlier estimate is usually better as compared with the earlier estimate. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: also oh-ver-uh-GAYNST for speakers who use /əˈɡeɪnst/; weak form — over loses its beat entirely and against reduces to /əˈɡɛn(t)s/, with the /t/ squeezed out between /n/ and /s/, so the phrase runs oh-ver-uh-GENS
entries.русский: напротив — устар., библ.; в книжн. речи также «в противопоставлении чему-либо»
entries.register: archaic and biblical in the spatial sense — the 1611 King James Version is where an American has met it (over against the treasury, over against the sepulchre), and nothing since has kept that sense alive. The contrastive sense is formal and scholarly and is still written today, chiefly in theology, philosophy, literary criticism, and continental-influenced social theory.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause: ✗ over against saying that. In the scholarly sense the object is characteristically an abstract noun — over against nature, over against the self, over against the state.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / sit / stand] over against [place] (archaic) · [define / set / place] [X] over against [Y] (scholarly) · [noun] over against [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: In the spatial sense it has simply been replaced: modern American English says across from, or opposite in a formal register. In the contrastive sense it competes with as against, as opposed to, and in contrast with, and it is the most bookish of the four — it carries a faint air of translated German philosophy, which is where much of its modern life comes from. Against against alone, which is opposition proper; over against sets two things side by side for comparison rather than putting one in conflict with the other.
entries.see also: opposite, across from, against, facing, as against, as opposed to

entries.meaning: Above something and looking down at it. Its whole meaning is what facing and above deliver together, which is why American listings reach for it any time there is a view to sell. The object is always the thing seen and never the viewer, and whatever does the overlooking is understood to have both a front and a vantage point — which is how the word came to work for terrain and fortifications as easily as for windows.
examples: They booked a room overlooking the courtyard. (1)
Her office is on the ninth floor, overlooking the river. (1)
We ate on a terrace overlooking the vineyard. (1)
The old fort sits on a bluff overlooking the harbor entrance. (2)
A water tower overlooking the interchange is the only landmark for miles. (2)
Guns were dug in along the ridge overlooking the valley floor. (2)

senses.head: Situated above and giving a view of
body: A deck overlooking the canyon.

senses.head: Standing high above and dominating, with no viewer implied
body: A ridge overlooking the highway.
examples: They booked a room overlooking the courtyard. (1)
Her office is on the ninth floor, overlooking the river. (1)
We ate on a terrace overlooking the vineyard. (1)
The old fort sits on a bluff overlooking the harbor entrance. (2)
A water tower overlooking the interchange is the only landmark for miles. (2)
Guns were dug in along the ridge overlooking the valley floor. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: oh-ver-LOOK-ing; four syllables, main stress on look; the vowel of look is the lax /ʊ/ of book, not the /u/ of Luke; the second syllable keeps the r-colored /ɚ/ in all American speech. Like every participial preposition it holds the full shape of the verb it came from, so there is no weak form — what fast speech does is compress the two unstressed syllables, not change their quality
entries.русский: с видом на; возвышающийся над
entries.register: neutral; the standard word in real-estate, hotel, and travel description
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — overlooking the bay, overlooking us. No clause of any kind, and no gerund: the thing seen is always a noun phrase (overlooking the harbor), never a verb (✗ overlooking swimming). The same warning that governs facing governs this word: the auditor is overlooking a whole account is the verb overlook in the progressive, not this preposition. The test is substitution — if with a view of can replace it without touching the rest of the clause, it is the preposition (a terrace overlooking the river → a terrace with a view of the river); if only failing to notice fits, it is the verb.
entries.pattern: [noun] overlooking [noun phrase] (a room overlooking the courtyard) · [be-verb] overlooking [noun phrase] · [sit / stand / perch] overlooking [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Overlooking is facing plus height. Both say which way the thing is turned, but overlooking adds that it is above what it sees and looks down at it: a room facing the harbor may be at sea level, a room overlooking the harbor is not. Against above, which is height with no view and no orientation at all — a floor can be above the lobby without seeing anything. Against over, which is height with alignment and no viewer. Against opposite and across from, which need a gap but neither elevation nor orientation. And keep the two lives of the word apart: as a preposition it gives you a view, as a verb it means you missed something — same form, opposite attitudes.
entries.see also: facing, above, over, opposite, atop

entries.meaning: Against the side of — of a blow, and nearly always a blow to the head. It is the narrowest preposition in this file: a single fixed frame, a single body part, and a single register. What earns it an entry is that learners meet it constantly in American dialogue, song lyrics, and comedy and have no way to parse it, because no dictionary sense of up or side predicts it. A figurative extension is now common — anything sudden and jarring can hit you upside the head.
examples: In a cartoon, the anvil catches him upside the head. (1)
Quoted speech: "Say that again and I'll smack you upside the head." (1)
Sports commentary: the ball caught the shortstop upside the ear. (1)
Comic narration: she popped him upside the head with a dish towel. (1)
Figurative: the diagnosis hit him upside the head and he sat down. (2)
Figurative: that last chapter comes upside your head out of nowhere. (2)
In edited prose the same event is written struck him on the side of the head. (1)

senses.head: Against the side of, of a blow — nearly always to the head
body: He got smacked upside the head with a rolled-up newspaper.

senses.head: Figurative: hitting someone suddenly and jarringly
body: The bill hit us upside the head in January.
examples: In a cartoon, the anvil catches him upside the head. (1)
Quoted speech: "Say that again and I'll smack you upside the head." (1)
Sports commentary: the ball caught the shortstop upside the ear. (1)
Comic narration: she popped him upside the head with a dish towel. (1)
Figurative: the diagnosis hit him upside the head and he sat down. (2)
Figurative: that last chapter comes upside your head out of nowhere. (2)
In edited prose the same event is written struck him on the side of the head. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: in the prepositional idiom the stress goes to the second syllable and the phrase runs straight into what follows, so upside the head comes out /ʌpˈsaɪ də ˈhɛd/ · up-SY-duh-HED. This is the opposite of the noun, which is stressed on the first syllable, /ˈʌpˌsaɪd/ · UP-syd (the upside of the deal), and which is a different word entirely
entries.русский: по (голове) — разг., афроамер. и южн.: об ударе сбоку, почти всегда по голове
entries.register: informal and regional. It belongs to African American English and to Southern American English, in one frame — upside the head — and from there it has spread through comedy, song, and quoted speech into general informal American usage. It never appears in edited expository prose, and outside its frame it is not used at all.
entries.type: simple (a compound of up + side, welded)
entries.complement: a noun phrase, and in practice almost always a possessed body part: upside his head, upside my face, upside the ear. No gerund, no clause. The narrowness of the complement is the entry's main fact — ✗ upside the fence, ✗ upside the door are not English, where against the fence and against the door are.
entries.pattern: [hit / smack / slap / knock / whack / pop] [object] upside [the head] · [get hit / catch one] upside the head
entries.contrast: Against against, the general word for contact under pressure, which takes any object and any register; upside is one idiom and one target. Against across, which is the neutral verb-frame for a blow to the face (hit him across the face) and cannot be swapped in here. Against on the side of, the flat paraphrase — hit him on the side of the head — which is what the same sentence becomes in a police report. And keep the homographs apart: the noun upside (an advantage, a gain) and the adverb phrase upside down have nothing to do with this preposition.
entries.see also: against, across, beside, alongside, on, over

entries.meaning: On or inside a vessel or a large vehicle. It covers both the static position and the act of getting there, which is why the same word does everyone aboard survived and she came aboard in Seattle. The figurative use — joining an organization — is a live metaphor that most writers now spell as two words.
examples: Everyone aboard the flight was accounted for. (1)
The equipment stayed aboard the research vessel all winter. (1)
She was the last passenger aboard the train. (1)
Welcome aboard — your badge is at the front desk. (2)
Two new engineers came aboard this month. (2)

senses.head: On or inside a ship, plane, train, or bus
body: There were forty-two passengers aboard the ferry.

senses.head: As a member of a crew, team, or organization (figurative)
body: We are glad to have you aboard the project.
examples: Everyone aboard the flight was accounted for. (1)
The equipment stayed aboard the research vessel all winter. (1)
She was the last passenger aboard the train. (1)
Welcome aboard — your badge is at the front desk. (2)
Two new engineers came aboard this month. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: uh-BORD; one stress, on the second syllable; the first syllable is always /ə/
entries.русский: на борту — на судне, в самолёте, поезде, автобусе; перен. в составе команды
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (all aboard, welcome aboard), which is how the word most often appears.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] aboard [vessel or vehicle] · [verb of motion] aboard [vessel] · aboard (adverb, no object)
entries.variants: on board (two words; identical in meaning, and the dominant form in the figurative business sense — bring her on board)
entries.contrast: Aboard is the vehicle-specific member of the in/on system: you are in a car, on a bus or a plane, and aboard a ship, a plane, a train, or a spacecraft — anything with an interior you can walk around in. It is more formal than either, which is why it belongs to announcements and news copy. Note the split with the two-word on board: for the figurative sense of joining a team, American English overwhelmingly writes on board, and aboard sounds nautical.
entries.see also: inside, within, on, in, astride

entries.meaning: In the middle of something that is treated as a mass rather than counted. The physical sense is literary and slightly old-fashioned in speech, but the abstract one is everywhere in news writing, where amid is the standard way to hang a story on a backdrop of continuing conditions without claiming a causal link.
examples: They found the ring amid the ashes. (1)
A single lit window amid all that darkness. (1)
Shares fell amid growing concern about the supply chain. (2)
The mayor resigned amid questions about the contract. (2)
Talks resumed amid signs that both sides were tiring. (2)

senses.head: Surrounded by, in the middle of a mass
body: A cabin amid the pines.

senses.head: Against a background of continuing events or conditions
body: The bill passed amid fierce opposition.
examples: They found the ring amid the ashes. (1)
A single lit window amid all that darkness. (1)
Shares fell amid growing concern about the supply chain. (2)
The mayor resigned amid questions about the contract. (2)
Talks resumed amid signs that both sides were tiring. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: uh-MIDST; both keep the schwa in the first syllable
entries.русский: среди, посреди — книжн.: окружённый сплошной массой, а не счётной группой; на фоне событий
entries.register: formal or literary in the physical sense; standard journalism in the background-events sense
entries.complement: noun phrase — characteristically a mass noun or a plural (amid the wreckage, amid rising costs). No clause, no gerund. A that-clause after amid speculation belongs to the noun speculation, not to amid.
entries.pattern: amid [mass noun] · amid [plural noun phrase] · amid [event noun] (amid the confusion)
entries.variants: amidst — chiefly British and slightly more literary; American English prefers amid, and the two are otherwise identical
entries.contrast: The amid/among split is countability. Amid surrounds you with something undifferentiated — wreckage, smoke, chaos, rumors taken as a mass; among surrounds you with individuals you could point at. Amid the crowd treats the crowd as a texture; among the crowd invites you to pick out faces. Amid also does something among cannot: set a scene of ongoing events behind a piece of news (amid falling revenues), which is now its most frequent use in print. The emphatic long form is in the middle of or in the midst of.
entries.see also: among, between, within, in the middle of, throughout

entries.meaning: Surrounded by or included in a group of more than one. Its four senses all follow from that: physically in the middle of a group, a member of a set, a share distributed to a group, and a trait holding across a group. The one hard requirement is plurality — whatever follows among must be countable as more than one or collective in meaning.
examples: We found him among the crowd at the gate. (1)
A few red maples stood out among all the oaks. (1)
Her novel is among the best things published that year. (2)
Among other duties, he handles scheduling. (2)
Split the tips evenly among the servers. (3)
The land was parceled out among six families. (3)
Turnout was highest among voters over sixty. (4)
Sleep problems are widespread among shift workers. (4)

senses.head: In the middle of, surrounded by a group
body: The cabin sits among the pines.

senses.head: Included in a set; one of
body: She is among the three finalists.

senses.head: Distributed to the members of a group
body: The estate was divided among the four children.

senses.head: Holding across the members of a group
body: The habit is common among first-year students.
examples: We found him among the crowd at the gate. (1)
A few red maples stood out among all the oaks. (1)
Her novel is among the best things published that year. (2)
Among other duties, he handles scheduling. (2)
Split the tips evenly among the servers. (3)
The land was parceled out among six families. (3)
Turnout was highest among voters over sixty. (4)
Sleep problems are widespread among shift workers. (4)

entries.pronunciation note: uh-MUNGST; the first syllable is always /ə/ and never carries stress
entries.русский: среди, между — в окружении группы из трёх и более; в числе; распределяя между всеми
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a plural, collective, or mass noun phrase — among the trees, among the staff, among us. Among the tree is ungrammatical: the object must denote more than one thing. Objective pronouns only (among them, among us). No clause, no gerund.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] among [plural noun phrase] · [divide / share / distribute] [object] among [plural noun phrase] · among [plural] (common among teenagers) · among other things
entries.variants: amongst — chiefly British; it is not wrong in American English but it is markedly bookish, and edited American prose uses among
entries.contrast: The schoolroom rule "between for two, among for more" is only half true. Between is correct for any number when the parties are individually in view and the relation is one-to-one — a treaty between six nations is perfectly standard. Among is the word when the group is an undifferentiated mass — the money was divided among the heirs treats them as a pool, between the two heirs names them. Against amid: among counts its objects, amid does not. Against within: within bounds a limit, among surrounds with members.
entries.see also: between, amid, within, inside, throughout

entries.meaning: In the space, the interval, or the relationship separating two or more distinct things that are individually in view. That last clause is what really governs the word — between keeps its objects separate and named, which is why it works for gaps, for treaties, for choices, and for joint efforts, and why it is fine with six parties as long as you can point at each one.
examples: A narrow gap between the fence and the shed lets the water through. (1)
She was sitting between her two brothers. (1)
Call me between nine and eleven. (2)
There were four collisions on that stretch between January and March. (2)
The treaty between the six nations took a decade to draft. (3)
Whatever is said between you and me stays here. (3)
He had to choose between the job in Denver and the one in Austin. (4)
There is not much to choose between the two proposals. (4)
Between them they own half the block. (5)
Between the deposit and the first month's rent, it came to three thousand. (5)

entries.pronunciation note: buh-TWEEN; the clipped literary form 'tween /twin/ survives only in poetry and in 'tween decks
entries.русский: между — между двумя или несколькими названными по отдельности объектами (ср. among)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a plural noun phrase (between the buildings), or ✗ two or more noun phrases joined by and — never by or. Objective pronouns only: between you and me, never between you and I. Gerunds are fine as coordinates (torn between working and commuting), and so are fused relatives: the difference between what he said and what he did. ✗ Never a that-clause — ✗ between that he called and that he wrote. Also an adverb with no object at all (a fence with a gate in between, the years between), and the preposition always has one.
entries.pattern: between [X] and [Y] · between [plural noun phrase] · between [pronoun] and [pronoun] · in between [noun phrase]
entries.variants: betwixt (archaic — see its own entry)
entries.first: between you and I is wrong. A preposition takes the objective case, and coordination does not change that — between you and me, between him and her. ✗ Second: the coordinator must be and. Choose between the red or the blue should be between the red and the blue. ✗ Third: ranges take and, not to. Between 1990 to 1995 is an error; write between 1990 and 1995 or from 1990 to 1995. On the between/among question, see that entry: the deciding factor is whether the parties are individually in view, not how many there are. The temporal sense is treated in time.
entries.contrast: Three errors cluster here, and all three are worth memorizing.
entries.see also: among, amid, betwixt, within, between (time)

entries.meaning: An archaic form of between, kept alive by poetry, by deliberate period flavor, and by one surviving idiom. Learners should be able to recognize it in older texts and should not produce it. Note that the idiom betwixt and between has drifted away from the preposition entirely and now works as an adjective phrase.
examples: The old deed describes the parcel as lying betwixt the river and the road. (1)
There is little to choose betwixt the two, as an older writer would have put it. (1)
Betwixt dawn and full light the whole field was white with frost. (1)
She has quit one job and not started the next, so she is betwixt and between. (2)
The design is betwixt and between — too plain for a gallery, too fussy for a kitchen. (2)

senses.head: Archaic or literary: between
body: The valley lies betwixt two ranges.

senses.head: In the fixed phrase betwixt and between: undecided, in an awkward middle state
body: He is betwixt and between about the move.
examples: The old deed describes the parcel as lying betwixt the river and the road. (1)
There is little to choose betwixt the two, as an older writer would have put it. (1)

She has quit one job and not started the next, so she is betwixt and between. (2)
The design is betwixt and between — too plain for a gallery, too fussy for a kitchen. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: buh-TWIKST
entries.русский: меж, между — устар., книжн.; живо лишь в обороте betwixt and between «ни то ни сё»
entries.register: archaic and literary; alive in modern American English only in the fixed phrase betwixt and between
entries.complement: the same as between — a plural noun phrase or two noun phrases joined by and, with objective pronouns. No clause, no gerund.
entries.pattern: betwixt [X] and [Y] · betwixt [plural noun phrase] · betwixt and between (fixed idiom)
entries.contrast: Betwixt is between in period costume. It means exactly the same thing and has no context in which it is the better choice for ordinary prose — using it in a business memo reads as a joke or an affectation. The one exception is the reduplicated idiom betwixt and between, meaning undecided or in an awkward middle state, which is still current and is not replaceable by between and between. Compare ere, the archaic before, which behaves the same way.
entries.see also: between, among, amid, ere, within

entries.meaning: Containing something as its residents or its permanent features. The frame is the workhorse of descriptive writing about places: a country is home to a population, a park is home to a species, a small city is home to a university and two museums. It is on the edge of the preposition class — home is still recognizably a noun — but it behaves as a fixed unit, cannot be modified from inside, and is worth learning whole.
examples: The refuge is home to the largest heron rookery in the state. (1)
Three counties home to fewer than ten thousand people share one hospital. (1)
The reef is home to several species found nowhere else. (1)
The campus is home to the country's oldest astronomy department. (2)
That block is home to two theaters and a dozen restaurants. (2)
The warehouse district was once home to the packing industry. (3)
Reversed and wrong: ✗ the herons are home to the marsh. Correct: the marsh is home to the herons. (1)

senses.head: Containing as residents or inhabitants
body: The island is home to about four hundred people.

senses.head: Containing as a permanent institution, business, or feature
body: The old bank building is now home to a bookstore.

senses.head: Formerly containing, in the frame once home to
body: The lot was once home to a cannery.
examples: The refuge is home to the largest heron rookery in the state. (1)
Three counties home to fewer than ten thousand people share one hospital. (1)

The campus is home to the country's oldest astronomy department. (2)

The warehouse district was once home to the packing industry. (3)
Reversed and wrong: ✗ the herons are home to the marsh. Correct: the marsh is home to the herons. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — to is never stressed here and reduces to /tə/ before a consonant and /tu/ before a vowel, so home to a colony of bats is /ˈhoʊm tu ə ˈkɑləni əv ˈbæts/ · HOHM-too-uh-KAH-luh-nee-uv-BATS, and home to three museums is HOHM-tuh-THREE-myoo-ZEE-umz
entries.русский: быть домом для — где живут люди или животные, где размещается учреждение
entries.register: neutral; it is the standard frame in journalism, tourism copy, natural history, and reference writing, and it is common in speech
entries.type: marginal (a predicative noun, home, welded to to and behaving as a unit)
entries.complement: noun phrase only — the residents or the contents. No gerund and no clause: ✗ home to manufacturing cars — write home to a car plant. The object may be a bare plural (home to wolves), a number phrase (home to 40,000 people), or a definite noun phrase (home to the state's oldest courthouse).
entries.pattern: [place] is home to [noun phrase] · [place noun] home to [noun phrase] (reduced relative: a valley home to three villages) · once home to / still home to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The direction is fixed, and reversing it is the standard learner error. The place is the subject and the inhabitants are the object: the marsh is home to herons, never ✗ the herons are home to the marsh. The test is substitution — if houses or is the home of fits, the frame is right. Watch the word-class trap as well: in he went home to his family, home is a directional adverb and to his family a separate phrase, and houses cannot be substituted; that is not this preposition. Against inside and within, which put one thing in another with no idea of residence, and against houses, the plain verb that does the same job in one word.
entries.see also: within, inside, in, throughout, among

entries.meaning: Down inside a mass of things and surrounded by them. It is among with the immersion made explicit, and the extra word does real work: it tells you the thing is not merely one of the group but tangled up in it, mixed through it, or lost in it. That is why it is the natural phrase for searching, for things growing in a jumble, and for whatever has ended up somewhere it does not belong.
examples: Bluebells come up in among the ferns every April. (1)
She keeps the good photographs in among the tax records, which is why nobody finds them. (2)
There were two counterfeit bills in among the deposit. (2)
The dog went straight in among the sheep and had to be called off. (3)
He was somewhere in among the crowd at the gate. (1)
Compare: a note among the papers is one of them; a note in among the papers is buried in them. (1)

senses.head: Mixed into and surrounded by a mass of things
body: Wildflowers grow in among the rocks.

senses.head: Hidden or lost in a mass of things
body: The lease is in among those files somewhere.

senses.head: Moving down into a crowd or a thicket
body: He waded in among the reeds to free the line.
examples: Bluebells come up in among the ferns every April. (1)
She keeps the good photographs in among the tax records, which is why nobody finds them. (2)
There were two counterfeit bills in among the deposit. (2)
The dog went straight in among the sheep and had to be called off. (3)
He was somewhere in among the crowd at the gate. (1)
Compare: a note among the papers is one of them; a note in among the papers is buried in them. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — in is unstressed /ɪn/ and the whole phrase carries one beat, on the second syllable of among, so it runs as a single word: in-uh-MUNG. Before a vowel the /n/ links forward — in among old letters is i-nuh-MUNG-old-LET-erz
entries.русский: среди, вперемешку с — разг.: затерявшись внутри массы предметов
entries.register: neutral, leaning conversational; edited prose often trims it to plain among, which is not quite the same thing
entries.complement: a plural or collective noun phrase, or an objective pronoun — in among the rocks, in among them. No gerund, no clause. A singular count noun is wrong: ✗ in among the box, ✗ in among the crowd member.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / find / lose / grow] in among [plural noun phrase] · [noun] in among [plural noun phrase]
entries.variants: in amongst — chiefly British, and markedly bookish in American English (see amongst); down in among and back in among add a further direction
entries.contrast: The in is not padding. Among distributes something across a group and says no more; in among puts it down inside the mass, mixed in and hard to pick out. A receipt among the papers is one of the papers; a receipt in among the papers is buried in them. Against amid, which is formal and wants a mass noun or an abstract event; in among is spoken and wants countable plurals. Against inside, which needs a container with a boundary — a pile of rocks has no inside, but you can still be in among them. Against between, which keeps its objects separate and named.
entries.see also: among, amid, between, inside, within, throughout

entries.meaning: At the point equally distant from the edges of something. It is the precise member of the middle family and it earns that precision honestly — a florist, a surveyor, and a page designer all mean the same thing by it. Its second sense, the busiest part of a town, is a mild extension of the same geometry and is the one American speech uses most.
examples: There is a drain in the center of the garage floor. (1)
Put the fold line exactly in the center of the page. (1)
A fountain stands in the center of the plaza. (1)
He found a spot right in the center of the third row. (1)
Parking is impossible in the center of the city on a weekday. (2)
The hotel is in the center of the historic district. (2)
Figurative, and therefore at rather than in: she was at the center of the whole negotiation. (2)

senses.head: At the point equally distant from the edges of
body: She set the cake in the center of the table.

senses.head: In the busiest or most built-up part of a place
body: Their office is in the center of town.
examples: There is a drain in the center of the garage floor. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — in /ɪn/, the /ðə/, and of /ə/ before a consonant, with the only beat on cen-: in the center of the room is /ɪn ðə ˈsɛnɚ ə ðə ˈrum/ · in-thuh-SEN-er-uh-thuh-ROOM, since ordinary American speech drops the /t/ of center after the /n/
entries.русский: в центре, посередине — на равном расстоянии от краёв; в центральной части города
entries.register: neutral. The American spelling is center; centre is British and appears in American text only inside proper names (Lincoln Centre is a name, not a spelling choice).
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — in the center of the table, in the center of it. No gerund and no clause: ✗ in the center of arguing about it.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / sit / stand / place] in the center of [noun phrase] · [noun] in the center of [noun phrase] · right / dead / smack in the center of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: in the middle of is the everyday word (see in the middle of); at the center of is the figurative form; in the heart of is the warmer version for towns and districts
entries.contrast: Two lines matter here. The first is in against at: in the center of the room is a physical position, while at the center of the investigation is a role — the figurative sense takes at, and mixing them produces the odd ✗ in the center of the scandal. The second is center against middle: in the middle of is vaguer and makes no claim about equal distance from the edges, so a table can be in the middle of a room without being in its center, and only middle works for stretches of time (in the middle of the night, not ✗ in the center of the night). Against amid and among, which say "surrounded by" and say nothing about the geometric middle.
entries.see also: in the middle of, amid, among, within, inside, throughout

entries.meaning: Within the bounds of a container, a building, or a boundary, with the boundary itself in the picture. It is the emphatic counterpart of in and the exact opposite of outside, and it keeps that contrast in every sense — a physical interior, the interior of an organization, and, in one informal American use, the interior of a stretch of time.
examples: Everything you need is inside the blue folder. (1)
Wait inside the building until they call your name. (1)
Sources inside the agency describe a very different timeline. (2)
The decision was made inside the family, not by the board. (2)
The whole repair was done inside of twenty minutes. (3)
If we leave now we'll be there inside of two hours. (3)

body: The receipt is inside the envelope.

senses.head: Within an organization, as opposed to outside it
body: The leak came from someone inside the department.

senses.head: In less than a stated period of time (informal, usually inside of)
body: They had it running again inside of an hour.
examples: Everything you need is inside the blue folder. (1)
Wait inside the building until they call your name. (1)

The whole repair was done inside of twenty minutes. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: in-SYD; stress distinguishes the parts of speech: preposition and adverb /ɪnˈsaɪd/ in-SYD, noun and attributive adjective /ˈɪnsaɪd/ IN-syd (an inside job)
entries.русский: внутри, в — в пределах вместилища; внутри организации, в отличие от посторонних
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (come inside), a noun (the inside of the lid), and an adjective (inside information); the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] inside [noun phrase] · [verb of motion] inside [noun phrase] · inside of [period of time] · stranded: the box it was inside
entries.variants: inside of — informal in the spatial sense (drop the of in edited prose); idiomatic and standard in the time sense, inside of an hour
entries.contrast: Against in: in is the neutral container word, inside insists on the enclosure and implies a contrasting outside. Both work for in / inside the box, but only in can go abstract — in trouble, in love, in a hurry have no inside version. Against within: inside is physical enclosure, within is limits and abstractions (within the law, not inside the law). And against into: inside is where something is, into is where it is going. The parent pair splits the same way — in is position, into is motion (she was in the office / she walked into the office) — with a short list of fixed phrases where in survives with a motion verb (put it in the drawer, throw it in the trash).
entries.see also: outside, within, in, inside of, aboard

entries.meaning: Beyond the bounds of something — a building, a boundary, a jurisdiction, or a scope. The physical sense is the base; the scope sense (outside my expertise, outside the law) is where the word does most of its work in adult prose, because it draws a limit and puts something firmly past it.
examples: There were reporters outside the building all afternoon. (1)
The house sits just outside the city limits. (1)
Anything over a hundred pounds is outside the elevator's rating. (2)
Enforcement of that rule is outside our authority. (2)
Outside of the opening chapter, the book holds up. (3)
Outside of Tuesday, I'm free all week. (3)

body: He was waiting outside the courthouse.

senses.head: Beyond the scope, limits, or authority of
body: That question is outside my expertise.

senses.head: Apart from, other than (usually outside of)
body: Outside of a cracked screen, the phone is fine.
examples: There were reporters outside the building all afternoon. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: owt-SYD; stress distinguishes the parts of speech: preposition and adverb /ˌaʊtˈsaɪd/ owt-SYD, noun and attributive adjective /ˈaʊtˌsaɪd/ OWT-syd (the outside lane)
entries.русский: снаружи, вне, за пределами — вне границ; вне компетенции; кроме (outside of)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund in the "apart from" sense only, and there almost always with of — outside of being tired, I'm fine. No clause of any kind, and never a that-clause. Also an adverb (wait outside), a noun (the outside of the house), and an adjective (an outside chance); the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] outside [noun phrase] · [verb] outside [noun phrase] · outside of [noun phrase] · outside [abstract limit] (outside the law)
entries.variants: outside of — extremely common in American speech; edited prose drops the of for the spatial and scope senses, but keeps it for the "apart from" sense, where besides or apart from is cleaner still
entries.contrast: The mirror image of inside, and it inherits the same rules: physical and scope senses only, with the abstractions handed to other words. On outside vs. outside of: American speech uses both freely, but editors delete the of in he waited outside the courthouse. The "apart from" sense (outside of a few complaints, it went fine) is the one place the of is normal — and it is also the place where apart from or besides reads better.
entries.see also: inside, beyond, without, outside of, besides

entries.meaning: Inside the limits of something. The limits are the point: within always implies a boundary you have not crossed, whether that boundary is a city line, a budget, a tolerance, a deadline, or the edge of an organization. It is the preposition of not-exceeding, and that is why contracts, specifications, and regulations lean on it so heavily.
examples: Everything within the fence line belongs to the county. (1)
The site is within a mile of the river. (1)
The project finished within budget by about four percent. (2)
Keep the reading within tolerance or the batch is rejected. (2)
Payment is due within thirty days of invoice. (3)
She had three offers within a week of posting her resume. (3)
The split within the party is wider than it looks. (4)
He kept the anger within himself for years. (4)

body: The house is within the historic district.

senses.head: Inside a range or a measured limit
body: The part came in within a thousandth of an inch.

senses.head: Before a stated period has elapsed (see also time)
body: Respond within ten business days.

senses.head: Inside a person, a group, or an organization
body: There is real disagreement within the committee.

entries.pronunciation note: with-IN; the th is voiced /ð/, as in this, not the /θ/ of thin; weak /wəˈðɪn/ — wuh-THIN
entries.русский: внутри, в пределах — в границах области, диапазона или срока
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund — write within the limits that the statute sets, never within the statute sets. Also an adverb (inquire within), which is the form on old shop signs.
entries.pattern: within [bounded area] · within [distance or measure] · within [period of time] · within [organization or person]
entries.contrast: The heart of this entry is in versus within, and in the time sense the difference has legal force. In three days means three days from now; within three days means at any point before three days have elapsed — a deadline, not a date. Spatially, in locates and within bounds: in the city says where you are, within the city limits says which side of a line you are on. Against inside: inside is physical enclosure, within is limits, ranges, and abstractions. The temporal sense is developed further in time.
entries.see also: inside, in, among, throughout, within (time)

entries.respell: with-OWT; the th is voiced /ð/; weak /wəˈðaʊt/
entries.meaning: Outside of, beyond the bounds of. This was once the ordinary opposite of within, and the two words still show their shared architecture. It survives in scripture, in older legal descriptions of land, in hymn and poetry, and in the frozen pair within and without. Recognize it; do not write it.
examples: The old charter refers to the parishes without the walls. (1)
They buried him without the churchyard, as the custom then required. (1)
A green hill far away, without a city wall. (1)
The ship was rebuilt within and without. (2)
She was calm within and without, whatever it cost her. (2)

body: The camp lay without the city gates.

body: The house was repainted within and without.
examples: The old charter refers to the parishes without the walls. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: wuh-THOWT
entries.русский: вне, за пределами — устар., книжн. в этом пространственном значении: вне городских стен
entries.register: archaic or literary in this spatial sense; the modern "lacking" sense is fully neutral and lives in accompaniment and exception
entries.complement: in the spatial sense, a noun phrase only — without the walls, without the gates. No clause, no gerund in this sense. Also an adverb in the fixed pairing within and without.
entries.pattern: without [walls / gates / city] (archaic spatial) · within and without (fixed adverbial pair)
entries.contrast: This entry covers only the obsolete sense "outside of," which is the exact opposite of within and is the reason the two words are built from the same halves. In living American English that job belongs entirely to outside; without the city now reads as a Bible verse or a history book, and a modern reader will hear the "lacking" sense instead and be confused. The productive modern sense — without money, without asking — is treated in accompaniment and exception and is not repeated here.

entries.meaning: Farther toward the stern than something else, aboard a vessel. The word divides a ship along its length and is precise about it: everything between the reference point and the stern is abaft that point. Its one non-shipboard use is the bearing phrase abaft the beam, which cuts the horizon in half at right angles to the keel and puts anything in the rear half abaft the beam — the phrase a lookout, a navigator, or a racing sailor actually uses.
examples: The crew quarters are abaft the mainmast. (1)
Everything abaft the funnel was damaged in the fire. (1)
Stow the spare anchor abaft the cockpit. (1)
A tanker showed up broad on the quarter, well abaft the beam. (2)
With the breeze abaft the beam she made eight knots easily. (2)
Adverb, no object, and therefore not this preposition: the sea was running abaft. (3)
Ashore the same idea is simply behind: the storeroom behind the office, not ✗ abaft the office. (1)

senses.head: Farther toward the stern of a vessel than

senses.head: In the bearing phrase abaft the beam: in the rear half of the horizon as seen from the ship
body: The wind was two points abaft the beam.

Ashore the same idea is simply behind: the storeroom behind the office, not ✗ abaft the office. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: also /əˈbɑft/ · uh-BAHFT in older American and in British speech; two syllables, stress on the second, and the first is already the reduced /ə/, so there is no further weak form
entries.русский: позади, ближе к корме, чем — мор. термин; за пределами флота устар.
entries.register: nautical technical, and archaic everywhere else. It is live, ordinary, and unremarkable in seamanship, naval writing, sailing instruction, and marine survey; outside that world it is costume, and a reader will hear it as pirate diction rather than as English.
entries.type: compound (a- + baft, itself Old English be + æftan "behind")
entries.complement: noun phrase — in practice a part of a vessel or a bearing: abaft the beam, abaft the mainmast, abaft the bridge. No gerund, no clause. It is also an adverb (the wind hauled abaft), which takes no object; that is the form most often heard on deck.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] abaft [part of a vessel] · [noun] abaft [part of a vessel] · abaft the beam · well abaft [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The pair to learn is abaft against astern of, and the difference is whether you are on the ship. Abaft is a position on board, farther toward the stern than the thing named — the galley can be abaft the mast. Astern of is a position in the water behind the whole vessel — the tender lies astern of the yacht. Its live opposite is afore (see afore), "farther forward than," which survives in the same nautical corner and nowhere else. Against behind, the ordinary word, which knows nothing about bows and sterns and is what a passenger would say.
entries.see also: astern of, behind, aboard, afore, past, beyond

entries.meaning: Behind a vessel, in the water it has passed through. The word is stern with the old a- prefix, and adding of is what turns the adverb into a preposition and gives it an object. Two uses account for nearly all of it: the physical one, where a tow, a tender, or a following ship lies astern of something, and the competitive one, where a boat that has lost ground is astern of the leader.
examples: The tender lay astern of the yacht all afternoon. (1)
Keep well astern of the dredge until it signals. (1)
A second freighter came up half a mile astern of the first. (1)
The fleet strung out for three miles astern of the committee boat. (2)
He rounded the mark astern of two boats he had beaten all week. (2)
Adverb, no object, and therefore not this preposition: the harbor fell astern by noon. (1)
For a general reader the sentence is simply the barge was behind the tug. (1)

senses.head: Behind, in the water behind another vessel
body: The barge rode a hundred yards astern of the tug.

senses.head: Trailing another vessel in a race, a line, or a convoy
body: She finished two minutes astern of the leader.
examples: The tender lay astern of the yacht all afternoon. (1)
Keep well astern of the dredge until it signals. (1)
A second freighter came up half a mile astern of the first. (1)
The fleet strung out for three miles astern of the committee boat. (2)

Adverb, no object, and therefore not this preposition: the harbor fell astern by noon. (1)
For a general reader the sentence is simply the barge was behind the tug. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — the first syllable is the reduced /ə/ and of drops to /ə/ before a consonant, so astern of the ferry is /əˈstɚn ə ðə ˈfɛri/ · uh-STUR-nuh-thuh-FAIR-ee. The stressed vowel is the r-colored /ɚ/ of stern
entries.русский: за кормой, позади — мор.: следом за другим судном
entries.register: nautical technical. Neutral and ordinary inside sailing, shipping, racing, and naval writing; outside that field it is archaic-sounding and a general reader will substitute behind without thinking.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — another vessel, a buoy, a mark, a landmark. No gerund, no clause. Bare astern is an adverb (the wake astern, slow astern, look astern) and takes no object at all; the adverb is far commoner than this preposition and is what is heard on a bridge.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / lie / fall / drop] astern of [vessel] · [noun] astern of [vessel] · a mile astern of [vessel]
entries.variants: aft of is the common American yachting alternative and is drifting toward abaft's job as well; behind is the plain word for a non-nautical reader
entries.contrast: Against abaft, the pair to learn: abaft is on board, astern of is outside the hull in the water behind it. Against behind, which covers both and cares about neither. Against past and beyond, which put a thing on the far side of a landmark rather than in trail of a moving vessel. And note that the racing sense — one boat astern of another — is about order in a fleet, so it competes with behind in the standings sense of that word.
entries.see also: abaft, behind, past, beyond, aboard, alongside

entries.meaning: In front of, in the physical or figurative presence of. The spatial sense is the older one and has been largely displaced in speech by in front of, retreating into formal registers where its stiffness is an asset. Two live uses remain fully current: appearing before an authority, and a task or choice standing before a person.
examples: The witness appeared before the grand jury on Thursday. (1)
He knelt before the altar. (1)
In the alphabet, M comes before N. (2)
Safety comes before speed on this crew. (2)
The choice before us is not a comfortable one. (3)
A long winter lay before them. (3)

body: E comes before F.

senses.head: Facing someone as a task, choice, or prospect

entries.pronunciation note: buh-FOR, and in fast speech /bfɔr/ with the first vowel gone entirely
entries.русский: перед, пред — книжн., юр.: перед лицом суда; раньше в порядке следования
entries.register: formal, legal, ceremonial, or literary in the spatial sense; the temporal sense is neutral and lives in time
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. In the spatial sense there is no gerund — before leaving is the temporal before, not this one. Never a finite clause after the preposition; before he arrived is the subordinating conjunction, a different word class with the same spelling.
entries.pattern: [stand / appear / kneel] before [noun phrase] · [noun] before [noun phrase] (the task before us) · [X] comes before [Y] (order)
entries.contrast: In modern American English the ordinary spatial word is in front of, not before. He parked in front of the house is what people say; before the house sounds like a nineteenth-century novel. Spatial before survives in three places: courtrooms and hearings (the case before the judge), ceremony and scripture (before God), and the metaphor of a task or a choice facing someone (the decision before us). Watch the word-class trap too — before is a preposition with a noun phrase, a conjunction with a clause, and an adverb with nothing (I've been here before).
entries.see also: in front of, behind, opposite, ahead of, before (time)

entries.meaning: At the back of something, on the side away from the front or from the observer. From that position the word picks up four extensions that all preserve the geometry: falling back in a race or a schedule, standing back of someone in support, working back of a public event as its hidden cause, and putting an experience back of you in the past.
examples: There is a small yard behind the building. (1)
She hid the box behind a stack of paint cans. (1)
The Rangers finished nine games behind the leaders. (2)
He fell behind on rent after the layoff. (2)
The union is solidly behind the proposal. (3)
Get behind this or get out of the way. (3)
Investigators still do not know who was behind the transfer. (4)
There is a real grievance behind all the shouting. (4)
Those years are behind her and she does not discuss them. (5)
Once the audit is behind us we can hire again. (5)

body: The trash cans are behind the garage.

senses.head: Later or slower than; in arrears (see also time)
body: We're two weeks behind schedule.

senses.head: Supporting, backing
body: The whole department is behind her.

senses.head: Responsible for, as the hidden cause or agent
body: No one knows who was behind the leak.

entries.pronunciation note: buh-HYND; the /h/ can drop in very fast speech, giving /bəˈaɪnd/
entries.русский: за, позади — с задней стороны; отставая; стоящий за чем-то — как поддержка или причина
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund in the cause sense (the thinking behind closing the plant, the money behind building the arena). No finite clause — write behind the decision to close, never ✗ behind they decided to close, and never a that-clause. Also an adverb (he stayed behind) and a noun (informal); the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] behind [noun phrase] · [verb] behind [noun phrase] · behind [schedule / on rent] · behind [person] (support) · stranded: the door he was hiding behind
entries.variants: in back of, and bare back of — genuinely American alternatives for the spatial sense, common in speech and regionally strong. In back of the house is the wider of the two; bare back of the barn is Midland, Southern, and rural, and is the older form. Both are unknown in British English and both are avoided in formal writing, where behind is always available
entries.contrast: Against after: after orders things in time or sequence, behind places them in space or measures a lag. He arrived after me is sequence; he finished behind me is a gap. Against beyond and past, which put something on the far side of a thing rather than at its back. Note also the American variants in back of and bare back of, which are standard in speech and jarring to British ears, and the temporal sense (behind schedule), developed in time.
entries.see also: before, beyond, past, in front of, behind (time)

entries.meaning: On the far side of something, and by extension past any limit at all. It is one of the most abstractly productive prepositions in English: once the literal sense of "farther than" is in place, everything that can have a limit — repair, belief, control, expectation, dispute — can be beyond it. The frozen phrases (beyond repair, beyond belief, beyond doubt) are worth learning as units.
examples: There is nothing beyond the last cattle guard but sagebrush. (1)
The trail continues a half mile beyond the falls. (1)
Deliveries do not run beyond six o'clock. (2)
He stayed beyond his welcome by about two hours. (2)
The engine was beyond saving. (3)
That decision is beyond my authority. (3)
Her generosity went beyond anything the family asked for. (4)
The results exceeded the forecast beyond all reason. (4)
Beyond a short statement, the company has said nothing. (5)
I remember nothing beyond what I already told the officer. (5)

senses.head: On the far side of; farther away than
body: The hills beyond the river are all national forest.

senses.head: Later than a point in time
body: The party went on well beyond midnight.

senses.head: Outside the limits, scope, or reach of
body: The damage was beyond repair.

senses.head: More than; surpassing
body: The response went beyond anything we expected.

senses.head: Apart from, other than (usually in a negative)

examples: There is nothing beyond the last cattle guard but sagebrush. (1)
The trail continues a half mile beyond the falls. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: bih-YAHND and /bɪˈjɔnd/ bih-YAWND; weak /bəˈjɑnd/ · buh-YAHND
entries.русский: за, по ту сторону — дальше чего-либо; позже; вне пределов; сверх, больше чем
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (beyond saving, beyond repairing), or a wh-clause (beyond what she told us). Never a that-clause — beyond that she told us is ungrammatical. Also an adverb (the hills beyond) and a noun (the great beyond).
entries.pattern: [be-verb] beyond [noun phrase] · beyond [abstract limit] (beyond repair) · beyond [verb-ing] · beyond [wh-clause] · go beyond [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Against past: past is close and dynamic — just past the bank is a landmark you have almost reached; beyond is static and farther out, and it dominates the abstract senses that past barely touches. Against outside: both draw a limit, but outside draws a boundary around a category (outside my expertise), while beyond draws a threshold something has exceeded (beyond my ability). One grammatical point worth its own line: beyond is one of the prepositions that takes a wh-clause, which is why beyond what he admitted is fine while beyond that he admitted is not.
entries.see also: past, outside, behind, across, above

entries.meaning: On the far side of a landmark, reckoned from it. The positional sense is essentially how Americans give directions — everything is past the light, past the bank, just past the second stop sign — and it depends on a shared reference point in a way beyond does not. The same geometry then runs along scales instead of streets (past forty, past its expiration date), and a short frozen list (past caring, past saving, wouldn't put it past her) preserves the oldest sense of having gone beyond a limit for good.
examples: The mailbox is just past the church on the right. (1)
Their driveway is a hundred yards past the cattle guard. (1)
Go past the second stop sign and it's on your left. (1)
That pitcher is past his prime and everyone knows it. (2)
The milk is well past its date. (2)
She was past fifty before she learned to swim. (2)
He is past caring what the committee thinks. (3)
The transmission was past saving by the time they looked at it. (3)
I wouldn't put it past her to call the mayor herself. (3)

body: The clinic is two blocks past the light.

senses.head: Beyond a point on a scale, an age, or a stage of life
body: That pitcher is past his prime.

entries.pronunciation note: PAST; one syllable, full vowel; no weak form, though in connected speech the final /t/ drops before a consonant, giving /pæs/ — PASS (past the store). Homophonous with passed, which — helped by that /t/-dropping — is the source of the commonest spelling error involving this word.
entries.русский: мимо, за — дальше указанного ориентира; за пределом возраста или стадии
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: simple (from the old participle of pass)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund only in a short frozen list — past caring, past saving, past praying for — which is not a productive pattern (✗ past finishing the report). No clause of any kind. Also an adverb (he walked past), an adjective (the past year), and a noun (in the past) — only the preposition has an object, which is the test: he walked past is the adverb, he walked past the church is the preposition.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] past [noun phrase] · [noun] past [landmark] · just past [noun phrase] · past [abstract limit] (past caring) · put it past [someone]
entries.contrast: The spelling trap first: passed is the verb, past is everything else. We passed the church (verb) but we drove past the church (preposition) and the mailbox is past the church (preposition). If you can put did in front of it, you want passed. Against beyond: past is near and reckoned from a landmark you have just cleared, beyond is farther out and far more abstract. Note that past has three homes here: this positional entry, the motion sense in movement and direction, and the clock sense (ten past four) in time.
entries.see also: beyond, behind, by, past (motion), past (time)

entries.meaning: On the nearer side of a line, seen from where the speaker is. Everything else the phrase does grows out of that: a point in time can have a nearer side (this side of Christmas), a region can be treated as a boundary for the sake of a boast (the best pie this side of the Mississippi), and a quality can be approached without being reached (just this side of legal). The viewpoint is always the speaker's, which is why the phrase is useless in writing that has not established where the speaker stands.
examples: The county line runs this side of the creek, not past it. (1)
There is not a hardware store this side of the interstate. (1)
Nothing is getting shipped this side of Monday. (2)
She will not be back this side of the holidays. (2)
It is the best diner this side of the Rockies, according to the sign. (3)
That contract is just this side of legal. (4)
The whole plan is this side of a miracle, and it worked. (4)

senses.head: On the nearer side of a boundary, river, or line
body: Everything this side of the ridge drains into the bay.

senses.head: Before a point in time
body: We will not have an answer this side of the new year.

senses.head: In the boasting frame: anywhere nearer than a famous or distant place
body: The best barbecue this side of Memphis.

senses.head: Falling just short of a quality or a limit
body: His answer was just this side of rude.

entries.pronunciation note: the initial th is the voiced /ð/ of this, not the /θ/ of thick; weak form — of reduces to /ə/ before a consonant, so this side of the river is /ˈðɪs saɪd ə ðə ˈrɪvɚ/ · THISS-syd-uh-thuh-RIV-er, and in the idioms the whole phrase compresses to one beat on side
entries.русский: по эту сторону от — ближе границы; до (срока); почти, чуть не (this side of rude)
entries.register: neutral in the spatial sense; the superlative and "just short of" senses are idiomatic and informal, and belong to speech and to writing with a voice
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun in senses 1 to 3. No gerund and no clause. Sense 4 is the exception worth knowing: there the complement is characteristically an adjective or an adjective-like noun — just this side of legal, this side of rude, this side of a miracle — which is the one place the phrase escapes the noun-phrase rule, and it is a frozen idiom rather than a productive pattern.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] this side of [landmark] · [noun] this side of [landmark] · the best [noun] this side of [place] · just this side of [adjective]
entries.variants: on this side of is the fuller and equally standard form for the spatial sense; the other side of and the far side of are the converses; that side of takes the speaker's viewpoint away
entries.contrast: Against beyond and past, its two opposites: this side of the river is nearer than the river, beyond the river and past the river are farther. Against before, which orders things in a sequence rather than placing them on a map. For sense 4, against short of, the closest paraphrase — just this side of rude and just short of rude say the same thing, and short of is the one to use in writing that has no voice to spare. The time sense is developed in time.
entries.see also: beyond, past, before, behind, short of, outside

entries.meaning: Spanning something from one side to the other, or positioned on the far side of it. The static senses collected here are what is left when the motion drains out of the word: a bridge that has already crossed, a scar that already spans a cheek, a store that already sits on the other side of the street. The third sense — distribution over a whole area or population — is now heavy in business and news prose.
examples: There is a fallen pine across the driveway. (1)
A long scar ran across the back of his hand. (1)
They live across the street from us. (2)
Her office is across the hall. (2)
Costs rose across all six divisions. (3)
The policy applies across the entire system. (3)
He listened with his arms folded across his chest. (4)
She had a wool blanket across her knees for the whole drive. (4)

entries.pronunciation note: uh-KRAHS in cot/caught-merged speech; the first syllable is already the reduced /ə/ and never takes stress, so there is no further weak form; the spelling and pronunciation acrosst are nonstandard
entries.русский: через, поперёк; по ту сторону — с одной стороны на другую; по всей площади или группе
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (he swam across); the preposition takes an object. In the "facing" sense the object attaches to from: across from the school.
entries.pattern: [noun] across [noun phrase] (spanning) · across from [noun phrase] (facing) · across [area or group] (distribution) · [be-verb] across [noun phrase]
entries.variants: acrost, acrosst — dialectal and nonstandard; never write them
entries.contrast: Against through: across treats its object as a two-dimensional surface you cover the face of, through treats it as a three-dimensional medium you pass inside — across the field, through the woods. Against along: across cuts a line, along follows it. Contact is optional and the senses split on it: sense 1 usually has none (a bridge across the canyon), sense 4 always has it (arms folded across his chest). And note the Americanism that matters most here: across from is the everyday American way to say "facing," where British English uses opposite. The motion sense is in movement and direction.
entries.see also: along, across from, opposite, throughout, astride, across (motion)

entries.meaning: Following the length of something, or located at some point on that length. The senses are really one geometry seen at different scales — the whole line, a spot on it, or a line that exists only in the mind. What unites every use is that the object must be linear; the moment it is not, the sentence stops working.
examples: There are streetlights along the whole east side of the park. (1)
Fenceposts run along the property line for a mile. (1)
She lined the books up along the top shelf. (1)
Somewhere along Route 6 we missed the turn. (2)
The pipe froze at a joint along the north wall. (2)
The trail loses elevation gradually all along the ridge. (2)
The new proposal is along the same lines as last year's. (3)
Somewhere along the way the project lost half its budget. (3)
