entries.русский: вдоль, по — следуя длине чего-либо; где-то на протяжении; перен. на некоем отрезке пути
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — and the object must be something with length: a road, a river, a wall, a shelf, a route. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb and verb particle (come along, bring it along, move along), where it has no object at all.
entries.pattern: [noun] along [linear object] · [verb] along [linear object] · somewhere along [linear object] · all along [linear object]
entries.contrast: The object has to be long. Along the fence works; along the room does not, because a room has no line to follow — and the figurative objects obey the same rule, since a way, a line, a spectrum, and a continuum are all lines. Against across, which cuts the line rather than following it — walk along the beach is parallel to the water, walk across the beach runs from the water to the dunes. Against alongside, which requires two separate parallel things: you can walk along a wall while touching it, but you walk alongside someone. Watch the particle too: in bring it along, along has no object and is not a preposition.
entries.see also: alongside, across, around, down, along (motion)

entries.meaning: Encircling something, or scattered in its vicinity. From the circle come two useful extensions: getting to the far side by going around an obstruction, and — because a circle drawn around a number is a rough boundary rather than a point — approximation. It is one of the highest-frequency prepositions in American speech and one of the vaguest.
examples: They put a fence around the pool last spring. (1)
Twelve chairs were set around the long table. (1)
His papers were scattered around the office. (2)
Is there a hardware store around here? (2)
The entrance is around the back of the building. (3)
Her place is just around the corner from mine. (3)
It cost around three hundred dollars. (4)
Let's say around seven, give or take. (4)
The whole meeting was structured around risk. (5)
There are real questions around the timeline. (5)

entries.pronunciation note: uh-ROWND; in casual speech the first syllable can drop entirely, giving /ˈraʊnd/ — ROWND (often written 'round); the full form is /əˈraʊnd/
entries.русский: вокруг, по — со всех сторон; повсюду в; за (углом); примерно (о числе)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; also a bare number or clock time in the approximation sense (around noon, around fifty), and a gerund in the jargon sense 5 (questions around hiring contractors). No clause, and never a that-clause. Also an adverb (look around, stick around) and a particle; the preposition takes an object.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] around [noun phrase] · [noun] around [noun phrase] · around [number or time] · around here / there · around the corner
entries.variants: round — chiefly British for the physical senses; see its own entry
entries.contrast: Use around, not round, in American English for every physical sense: around the corner, around the table, around the block. For approximation, around and about are both American and interchangeable, with around commoner in speech and approximately the formal choice. Sense 5 — a conversation around funding — is business jargon that has spread fast and that many editors still delete in favor of about. The motion sense (drove around the lake) belongs to movement and direction, and the temporal approximation is treated in time.
entries.see also: round, about, near, throughout, around (motion)

entries.meaning: With one leg, one side, or one part on each side of something. The literal sense is equestrian, and the figurative sense keeps the geometry exactly: a town astride a highway has buildings on both sides of it. Strategic and geopolitical writing likes the word because it implies control of what passes between.
examples: He rode astride a borrowed mare all afternoon. (1)
The child sat astride his father's shoulders. (1)
The village lies astride the old post road. (2)
The refinery sprawls astride the county line. (2)
A single garrison stood astride the only pass. (2)

senses.head: With a leg on each side of something
body: She sat astride the fence rail.

senses.head: Extending on both sides of a line, route, or boundary
body: The town sits astride the state line.

entries.pronunciation note: uh-STRYD; the first syllable is always /ə/ and never stressed
entries.русский: верхом на; по обе стороны от — книжн.: ноги по обе стороны; по обе стороны линии
entries.register: formal or literary; common in journalism and military writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (she rode astride — that is, not sidesaddle).
entries.pattern: [sit / ride / stand] astride [noun phrase] · [place or thing] astride [line or route]
entries.contrast: Astride demands two sides straddled, which is exactly what across does not require: a bridge is across a river because it spans it, but a city is astride a border because it has territory on both sides. Over is the weaker word: it may cover a thing and even touch it (a blanket over the rail), but it never claims a leg or a side on each side of it, which is the entire content of astride (sitting astride the rail). And note the adverbial use, which carries a specific historical meaning in equestrian contexts — riding astride rather than sidesaddle.
entries.see also: across, over, atop, alongside, athwart

entries.meaning: The place where two streets, two walls, or two edges meet. It is the American address-giving phrase, and it is worth an entry chiefly for the at / on / in split, which learners get wrong in both directions — putting a shop in an intersection or a stain at the corner of a rug. The rule underneath is the ordinary one for these three: at is a point, on is a surface, in is an interior.
examples: Meet me at the corner of Fourth and Pine at six. (1)
The old hotel stood at the corner of Broadway and Ninth until 1978. (1)
There has been a light at the corner of Mill and Route 9 since the accident. (1)
A cot was set up at the corner of the gym nearest the door. (2)
The fence post at the corner of the lot has rotted through. (2)
Her initials are at the corner of every drawing. (3)
Compare the three: the deli sits on the corner of Ninth and Elm; meet me at the corner of Ninth and Elm; the mop is in the corner of the kitchen. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — everything but cor- is unstressed: at /ət/, the /ðə/, of /ə/ before a consonant. At the corner of Fifth and Main runs /ət ðə ˈkɔrnɚ ə ˈfɪfθ ən ˈmeɪn/ · uht-thuh-KOR-ner-uh-FIFTH-un-MAYN, with and reduced all the way to /ən/
entries.русский: на углу — на пересечении улиц; в углу страницы, экрана или помещения
entries.register: neutral — the standard American way to name a street intersection, in speech, in directions, and in print
entries.complement: noun phrase — characteristically two street names joined by and, or a single noun naming a bounded surface. No gerund, no clause: ✗ at the corner of turning onto Main.
entries.pattern: at the corner of [street] and [street] · at the corner of [room / field / page / lot] · [building] on the corner of [street] and [street]
entries.variants: on the corner of — used when the thing sits on the corner lot itself (the drugstore on the corner of Ninth and Elm); bare at plus the two street names (at Ninth and Elm) is the shortest and most idiomatic American form; at the corner of [street] at [street] is not English
entries.contrast: Three prepositions front the corner of and they do three different jobs. At the corner of names a point you can meet someone at or turn at. On the corner of puts a building on the corner lot. In the corner of puts a thing inside an angle — in the corner of the room, in the corner of my eye, in the corner of the drawer — and it is the only one of the three that requires an interior. A street intersection therefore takes at or on and never in: ✗ in the corner of Fifth and Main. Against at generally, of which this is the sharpened form: at Fifth and Main is the point sense of at, and at the corner of just names the point out loud.
entries.see also: at the edge of, kitty-corner from, across from, at, on, in

entries.meaning: At the outer boundary of an area or the rim of a surface — and, in the on variant, at the boundary of a condition. The literal sense is doing quiet geographical work all through American description: towns sit at the edge of counties, houses at the edge of woods, ice at the edge of a pond. The figurative sense is one of the language's main ways of saying that something has not happened yet but is about to.
examples: A row of cottonwoods grows at the edge of the pasture. (1)
Their subdivision sits at the edge of the county, half a mile from the line. (1)
Do not leave the glass at the edge of the counter. (2)
Ice was still forming at the edge of the pond in April. (2)
He was on the edge of tears by the end of the sentence. (3)
The whole department is on the edge of quitting over the schedule. (3)
That third act kept everybody on the edge of their seats. (4)

entries.pronunciation note: note the article — the is /ði/ before the vowel of edge, not the /ðə/ it takes before a consonant. Weak form — at reduces to /ət/ and of keeps its /v/ before a following vowel but drops to /ə/ before a consonant, so at the edge of the field is /ət ði ˈɛdʒ ə ðə ˈfild/ · uht-thee-EJ-uh-thuh-FEELD
entries.русский: на краю, у края — на границе участка, у обрыва; перен. на грани (on the edge of)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. A gerund is possible only in the on the edge of variant, and only in the figurative sense: on the edge of quitting, on the edge of losing the house. ✗ At the edge of quitting is not English. No clause of any kind.
entries.pattern: [be-verb / stand / stop / build] at the edge of [noun phrase] · [noun] at the edge of [noun phrase] · on the edge of [state or event] · on the edge of [verb-ing]
entries.variants: on the edge of — interchangeable with at the edge of for the literal senses (a house at / on the edge of the woods), and the only one of the two that carries the figurative sense of being close to a state: on the edge of collapse, on the edge of tears, on the edge of a breakthrough. The seat idiom is fixed with on: on the edge of your seat, never ✗ at the edge of your seat.
entries.contrast: Against on the verge of, the figurative twin and the more formal of the two — on the verge of bankruptcy is what the filing says, on the edge of bankruptcy what the interview says. Against outside and beyond: something at the edge of an area is still inside it, which is exactly what makes the phrase useful — a cabin at the edge of the forest is in the forest, a cabin outside the forest is not. Against near, which places a thing without reference to any boundary, and against at the end of, which needs a length or a sequence rather than an area.
entries.see also: at the corner of, outside, within, beyond, near, on the verge of

entries.respell: DOWN; one syllable, full diphthong; no reduced form
entries.meaning: At or toward a lower point on something, or simply farther along it. American usage has largely bleached the elevation out of the second sense — you go down to the corner store on flat ground — which leaves down functioning as a vague marker of distance from the speaker, paired with up in a way that is regional as much as geographic. Once distance along a line is all the word carries, it takes the last short step and starts measuring distance in time: down the road is next year.
examples: The trailhead is a quarter mile down the ridge. (1)
Water was running down the outside of the foundation. (1)
The pharmacy is two blocks down the street. (2)
His office is down the hall on the left. (2)
Her family is down south for the winter. (3)
We drove down the coast as far as Big Sur. (3)
He is third down the depth chart and unlikely to play. (4)
The Dodgers slid two spots down the standings in a week. (4)
That shortcut will cost somebody money down the road. (5)
Two owners down the line, nobody remembered the handshake deal. (5)

entries.pronunciation note: down destresses without changing its vowel, which is unusual for a preposition this frequent
entries.русский: вниз по; дальше по — ниже по склону; дальше по улице (амер. разг., без перепада высот)
entries.register: neutral; the "farther along" sense is characteristically American and informal
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Down is also an adverb (sit down), a verb particle (turn it down), an adjective (the server is down), a noun (third down, goose down), and a verb (downed the drink) — the preposition is the only one with an object, and the test is that you cannot move it: ran down the hill has no ran the hill down.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] down [linear object] · [verb] down [linear object] · down the street / road / hall · down south / down the coast
entries.contrast: Sense 2 is the one to learn: ✗ in American English down the street usually has nothing to do with elevation — it means "farther along, away from here," and down and along are nearly interchangeable there. Against below and under, which are pure vertical position with no path involved; down always implies a line you could travel. ✗ The British "attributable to" sense — that's down to the weather, it's down to you — is not American; Americans say because of, due to, or up to you. The motion sense is in movement and direction.
entries.see also: up, below, along, under, down (motion)

entries.meaning: No longer on, or at a remove from, something it was attached to or aligned with. entries.русский: с, от — снятый с поверхности; отходящий от (комната off the kitchen); в отдалении от берега
entries.register: neutral; off of is standard American speech and is deleted in edited prose
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (the lid came off), an adjective (the milk is off, his timing is off), a noun, a verb, and a very productive particle (call it off, put it off) — none of which takes an object, and the preposition always does: he is off is the adjective, he is off his game is the preposition.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] off [noun phrase] · [noun] off [noun phrase] (branching) · off the coast of [place] · off [substance] (abstaining) · off [standard] (off his game)
entries.variants: off of — ubiquitous in American speech, absent from edited prose; off from is nonstandard everywhere
entries.contrast: Two usage points. First, off of: get off the couch is the written form and get off of the couch is what people say — the of is redundant and editors remove it, but it is not a marker of poor speech in America the way it is in Britain. Second, off from is simply wrong; there is no such preposition. Against from, which names a source without implying prior contact — she took it from the shelf versus she took it off the shelf, where off says it was resting there. Sense 2 (a bedroom off the hallway) has no synonym and is worth learning on its own.
entries.see also: out, from, on, off (motion), off of

entries.respell: OWT; one syllable, full diphthong; no reduced form
entries.meaning: Through an opening to the outside, or along a route leading away from a center. Bare prepositional out is a narrow word with a strong American accent: it lives on windows, doors, and highways, and it hands everything else to out of. Its enormous life as an adverb, adjective, noun, and particle is separate and is not the preposition.
examples: Don't throw anything out the car window. (1)
He walked out the side door without a word. (1)
Smoke was pouring out the vent. (1)
Their place is a few miles out the old highway. (2)
The dogs are out back if you want to see them. (2)
Her people are all out west somewhere. (2)

entries.русский: наружу через — смотреть out the window «в окно»; дальше по дороге прочь от города
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a restricted noun phrase. As a bare preposition in American English, out takes essentially only openings (out the window, out the door, out the chimney) and a few direction and route nouns (out Route 9, out back, out west). For everything else, American English requires out of. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb (the fire went out), an adjective (the truth is out), a noun (a called third strike is an out), a verb (the story outed him), and a very productive particle (hand it out, figure it out) — none of which takes an object, and the preposition always does: he leaned out is the adverb, he leaned out the window is the preposition.
entries.pattern: [verb] out [opening] (look out the window) · [live / drive] out [route or direction] · out back / out west / out east
entries.variants: out of — the general-purpose form; see out of
entries.contrast: This is one of the sharpest American/British splits in the whole class. Americans say he leaned out the window; the British say out of the window, and out the window strikes them as substandard. In American English the bare form is not only acceptable but preferred with openings. Where the two agree: with containers, sources, and materials you need out of on both sides of the Atlantic — out of the box, out of money, made out of oak. Against outside, which is a static position rather than a passage through an opening.
entries.see also: out of, outside, off, inside, out (motion)

entries.meaning: Off to one side, across a short space. The static sense is the one that matters here: something over to the left or the right is displaced in that direction from where you are looking, without any motion at all. The motion sense — going over to a place — is the commoner one in speech, and it carries the same idea of a short, familiar crossing.
examples: The shutoff valve is over to the left of the meter. (1)
Slide the couch a little over to the window side. (1)
She came over to our table to say hello. (2)
Bring the kids over to the house on Sunday. (2)
He wandered over to the fence and looked at the horses. (2)
That's all from the studio — over to you, Marcus. (3)
Stranding: that's the desk he walked over to. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — to is never stressed and reduces to /tə/ before a consonant and /tu/ before a vowel, so over to the window is /ˈoʊvɚ tə ðə ˈwɪndoʊ/ · OH-ver-tuh-thuh-WIN-doh, and ✗ oh-ver-TOO is wrong in every context except a deliberate contrast. Over itself keeps its r-colored /ɚ/ and has no reduced form
entries.русский: в сторону; туда к — правее или левее от точки взгляда; подойти к; передать слово
entries.register: neutral and characteristically spoken American
entries.type: complex, and a contested one — see the complement note
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause. The word-class warning is the point of this entry: most grammars analyze over to as the adverb over followed by the preposition to — he walked over | to the desk — rather than as a single preposition. Two facts argue for treating it as a unit anyway. It resists interruption: he walked over quickly to the desk is a different reading, with over attached to the verb. And it survives with no verb of motion at all — the shutoff valve is over to the left — where nothing has moved and over cannot be a directional adverb. Note that it strands on to alone: the desk he walked over to is fine, and there is no ✗ the desk he walked to over.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] over to [noun phrase] · [be-verb] over to [the left / the right / one side] · over to [person] (handing a turn) · come over to [place]
entries.contrast: Against bare to: over adds the idea of crossing a space the speaker treats as small and familiar. Come to my place is neutral; come over to my place says you are nearby and coming across. Against across to, which insists on a definite thing crossed — a room, a street, a river. Against the parallel members of the same family, back to, down to, and up to, each of which adds its own direction to the same to. The motion sense proper belongs to movement and direction; what is kept in this file is the static use, the valve is over to the left, which is pure position and is the reason the phrase earns a place among the place prepositions at all.
entries.see also: over, across, to, over (motion), back to, up to

entries.meaning: A reduced form of around that became a separate word. In British English it is the ordinary preposition for encircling and vicinity; in American English it has been almost entirely displaced by around and remains only where it is locked into a compound or an idiom. examples: British usage: they sat round the kitchen table. American: around the kitchen table. (1)

Dispatchers staffed the line round the clock for six days. (2)
The resort is open year-round. (2)
We booked a round-trip out of Denver and drove from there. (2)

entries.register: chiefly British as a general preposition; in American English it survives only in fixed phrases
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — the same range as around. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb, adjective, noun, and verb, all of which are fully standard in American English; only the general prepositional use is British.
entries.pattern: round [noun phrase] (British) · American fixed forms only: round the clock, year-round, round-trip, round about · British, not American: round the bend, all round
entries.variants: around — the American form; use it everywhere except in the fixed phrases listed here
entries.contrast: Americans write around. Round the corner, round the table, and round the block are British; the American equivalents all take around. What American English keeps is a short list of frozen compounds and idioms where round is the only possible form: round the clock, year-round, round-trip, and the dated approximating round about. Do not take round the bend (crazy) or all-round for American forms — both are British, and the American equivalents are around the bend and all-around. Treat any other prepositional round in a text as a signal that the writer is British or is imitating speech.

entries.meaning: In every part of a space or a body. The word is built to be exhaustive — it claims completeness in a way in and across do not — which is why it belongs to inspection reports, specifications, and any prose that needs to say everywhere inside this thing, with no exceptions.

Smoke detectors are required throughout the residence. (1)

senses.head: In every part of an organization, a region, or a body

entries.pronunciation note: throo-OWT; the initial cluster is /θr/, not /tr/; stress falls on the second syllable, so in connected speech the first one reduces to weak /θrəˈaʊt/ — thruh-OWT
entries.русский: по всему, повсюду в — в каждой части помещения, региона или организации
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Also an adverb with no object at all (the house has hardwood throughout), which is a common and fully standard use.
entries.pattern: throughout [bounded space] · throughout [organization or region] · [noun phrase] ... throughout (adverb, no object)
entries.contrast: Against through: through traces a path in one side and out the other, throughout saturates every part with no path at all. Water ran through the house is a leak; there is water damage throughout the house is an insurance claim. Against all over, the spoken equivalent — toys all over the house and toys throughout the house mean the same thing at different registers. Against across, which distributes over a surface or a set rather than filling a volume. The temporal sense is developed in time.
entries.see also: within, across, around, among, throughout (time)

entries.meaning: On the left-hand side of something. It is one of the two phrases English uses to lay a scene out in a row, and its whole difficulty is the point of view: unlike above and below, which are fixed by gravity, left and right flip depending on which way the observer and the object are facing. Beyond the physical sense it does duty on any scale that runs left to right — a line of text, a number line, a timeline, a political spectrum.
examples: The extra chairs are stacked to the left of the piano. (1)
In the photograph, my grandmother is standing to the left of the porch rail. (1)
Park to the left of the blue truck and leave room for the gate. (1)
The exit is immediately to the left of the elevator bank. (1)
The footnote marker sits just to the left of the margin. (2)
Everything to the left of the cursor was deleted. (2)
The bill has support from members well left of center. (3)
Ambiguous without help: the scar is to the left of his nose — say his left or your left. (1)

senses.head: On the left-hand side of, as seen by the observer
body: The light switch is to the left of the door.

senses.head: Earlier in a row, a line of text, or a left-to-right scale
body: Every digit to the left of the decimal point is a whole number.

senses.head: In the phrase left of center: on the political left, with the article dropped
body: Her voting record is well left of center.
examples: The extra chairs are stacked to the left of the piano. (1)
In the photograph, my grandmother is standing to the left of the porch rail. (1)

Ambiguous without help: the scar is to the left of his nose — say his left or your left. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — to /tə/, the /ðə/, and of /ə/ before a consonant, with the only beat on left: to the left of the door is /tə ðə ˈlɛft ə ðə ˈdɔr/ · tuh-thuh-LEFT-uh-thuh-DOR. Before a vowel of keeps its /v/ (to the left of it)
entries.русский: слева от — с левой стороны для наблюдателя; левее в ряду или в записи числа
entries.register: neutral — the standard frame for describing a layout, a diagram, a photograph, a stage, or a screen
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause: ✗ to the left of parking the truck.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] to the left of [noun phrase] · [noun] to the left of [noun phrase] · just / immediately / directly / far to the left of [noun phrase] · left of [noun] (article dropped, technical and political)
entries.variants: left of with the article dropped is standard in technical and political writing — left of center, left of the decimal point, three characters left of the cursor; on the left of is chiefly British; at the left of is not idiomatic for position relative to another object, though at the left alone is fine for a region of a page
entries.contrast: The question the phrase never answers by itself is whose left. By default it is the observer's — the lamp to the left of the couch is left as you look at it. But an object with a front of its own imposes its own orientation: stage left is the performer's left and therefore the audience's right, and a patient's left is the doctor's right. When it matters, say from the audience's point of view or the patient's left, because the phrase alone will be read both ways. Against beside and next to, which give adjacency and no side at all. Against before and behind, the other axis. And note that left of center has been taken over by politics, so a purely spatial reading of it now needs help.
entries.see also: to the right of, beside, across from, before, behind, next to

entries.meaning: On the right-hand side of something. Everything said of to the left of applies here unchanged: the default is the observer's viewpoint, an object with a front of its own overrides it, and the phrase extends naturally to any left-to-right scale. The one extra hazard is the word right itself, which carries three unrelated meanings that show up in the same sentences.
examples: The recycling bin goes to the right of the back steps. (1)
In the family photo, the twins are to the right of my father. (1)
The freight elevator is immediately to the right of the loading dock. (1)
Take the second door to the right of the mural. (1)
Round anything more than two places to the right of the decimal. (2)
The column to the right of the totals is for initials. (2)
He ran a campaign well right of center and won the primary. (3)
Not this preposition: the utility has a right of way across the back lot. (1)

senses.head: On the right-hand side of, as seen by the observer
body: The thermostat is to the right of the hall closet.

senses.head: Later in a row, a line of text, or a left-to-right scale
body: The digits to the right of the decimal point are the cents.

senses.head: In the phrase right of center: on the political right, with the article dropped

entries.pronunciation note: weak form — to /tə/, the /ðə/, of /ə/ before a consonant, with the only beat on right: to the right of the stove is /tə ðə ˈraɪt ə ðə ˈstoʊv/ · tuh-thuh-RYT-uh-thuh-STOHV. Before a vowel of keeps its /v/, and the /t/ of right commonly flaps into it, giving RY-duv
entries.русский: справа от — с правой стороны для наблюдателя; правее в ряду или в записи числа
entries.register: neutral — the mirror of to the left of, and used in exactly the same places
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No gerund, no clause: ✗ to the right of loading the truck.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] to the right of [noun phrase] · [noun] to the right of [noun phrase] · just / immediately / directly / far to the right of [noun phrase] · right of [noun] (article dropped, technical and political)
entries.variants: right of with the article dropped is standard in technical and political writing — right of center, right of the decimal point; on the right of is chiefly British. Do not confuse the dropped-article form with the noun phrase right of in right of way, right of first refusal, and right of entry, where right is the noun meaning an entitlement and the phrase is not this preposition at all.
entries.contrast: The same point-of-view problem as its mirror, with the same solutions: stage right is the performer's right and the audience's left, and a patient's right is the examiner's left. Against to the left of, which is its exact opposite in every sense, including the political one. Against beside, which gives adjacency without a side. And note the trap the left-hand entry does not have: right is four different words in English — the direction, the entitlement, the adjective correct, and the intensifier (right next to the door) — and only the first is this preposition. In right next to the door, right is the intensifier and the preposition is next to.
entries.see also: to the left of, beside, across from, before, behind, next to

entries.meaning: At or toward a higher point on something, or simply farther along it in the direction the speaker treats as away. As with down, American usage has drained most of the elevation out of the everyday sense, leaving a vague directional marker that pairs with down and varies by region — New Yorkers go up to the Bronx, New Englanders up to Maine, and neither is about altitude. What is left of the vertical idea survives cleanly in rankings and in two idioms that keep an object and therefore keep the preposition: up your alley, up the creek.
examples: Their mailbox is halfway up the driveway. (1)
There's a crack running up the chimney. (1)
The laundromat is two doors up the street. (2)
She works at a shop up the road from here. (2)
We drove up the coast to Mendocino. (3)
His family summers up north on the lake. (3)
He worked his way up the ladder from the loading dock. (4)
The song climbed up the chart for six straight weeks. (4)
A restoration that size is right up his alley. (5)
If the loan falls through we are up the creek. (5)

senses.head: At a higher point on a slope or a vertical surface
body: The cabin is up the hill from the road.

senses.head: Farther along; away from here (no elevation implied)
body: He lives up the block from the school.

senses.head: Toward the north, or inland along a river or coast
body: They have a place up north.

senses.head: Higher in a ranking, a scale, or a sequence
body: She moved up the depth chart fast.

senses.head: In the fixed idioms up someone's alley and up the creek
body: A job like that is right up her alley.

entries.pronunciation note: the vowel is already the lax /ʌ/ and has nothing further to reduce to, so unstressed up simply loses its beat (up the street /ʌp ðə ˈstrit/) without changing quality. The same is true of its opposite, down. In up to, only the second word weakens: UP-tuh, never uh-TOO
entries.русский: вверх по; дальше по — выше по склону; дальше по улице; севернее, вверх по реке
entries.register: neutral; the "farther along" sense is characteristically American and informal
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun. No clause, no gerund. Up is also an adverb (stand up), a verb particle (look it up, ran up a bill), an adjective (the system is up), a noun (ups and downs), and a verb (upped the price). The particle/preposition test is movement: you can say ran a bill up but not ran the hill up, because in ran up the hill the hill is the object of the preposition.
entries.pattern: [be-verb] up [linear object] · [verb] up [linear object] · up the street / road / coast · up north
entries.contrast: The mirror of down, and it inherits the same American quirk: up the block usually implies no elevation at all, only distance in a direction the speaker treats as away. Against above and atop, which are static height with no path; up implies a line you could travel. The one thing to be careful about is the word class — up is far more often a particle than a preposition, and the movement test above settles it every time. The motion sense is in movement and direction.
entries.see also: down, above, atop, along, up (motion)
